### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in what passages of their works, commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the various branches of ecclesiastical learning.**

# [Mozarabic Liturgy according to the Rule of St. Isidore]

## [Col. 0009]

### Francis Anthony Lorenzana, Archbishop of Toledo, Primate of Spain, to the reader: greetings.

## [Col. 0009A]

From the beginning of this pastoral office of ours, nothing has been more deeply fixed in our mind than to follow the footsteps of our forebears, especially those of the most illustrious Cardinal Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros. He committed the nearly forgotten Gothic, or Mozarabic, rite to print so that the memory of the Gothic Fathers might return to posterity, and so that the honor due to Hosius, Leander, Fulgentius, Isidore, Braulio, Eugenius, Helladius, Julian, Ildephonsus, and the other Fathers who have served our Spanish land so well might, as it were, revive: those vigorous champions of the faith, the pillars of the Churches of Spain, the glory of the Gothic people, and the presidents of councils.

While diligently devoting ourselves to this work, we kept before our eyes and handled with our own hands very ancient Gothic codices breathing the fragrance of the old liturgy, written by hand nearly eight hundred years ago, and at least five hundred years before the sad birth of Luther, Calvin, their followers, and the innovators against the sacraments by which Holy Mother Church is wonderfully nourished and sustained—so that the enemies of the faith might be converted to better fruit, or at least, on reading the sacred mysteries in such ancient autographs, might fall silent.

The Roman Church, mother and teacher of all, labored with the utmost zeal so that the sacred liturgy might be celebrated throughout the world according to one and the same rite, and thus the prayer of all the faithful might be one. Nevertheless, it did not abolish the ancient Missals and Breviaries; rather, like a treasure in the sanctuary, it retains the Psalter according to the old Italic version, highly praised by Augustine and other Fathers. It chants it beforehand in the Vatican chapel and keeps its codices in the library as in a reliquary of the heart.

## [Col. 0009C]

The sacred Council of Trent itself, recognizing that the greatest benefit proceeded from this, decreed that religious orders which had used a particular rite for two hundred years before the Council could retain it both in the sacrifice of the Mass and in the celebration of the divine office. For this reason, supported by the longest prescription of time and by immemorial custom, the Cistercians, Carthusians, the barefoot hermits of Mount Carmel, and the Preachers of the Order of Saint Dominic observe their own rites and ceremonies. Thus, at the same time, the unity of the sacrifice shines forth in the Church of God, and the Bride of Christ, when the ancient Roman rite is compared with the more polished one, is surrounded by a wonderful variety.

## [Col. 0009D]

That outstanding Cardinal Ximénez, that Christian and statesmanlike hero, inflamed with zeal for the faith, gathered the Gothic, Isidorian, or Mozarabic codices scattered everywhere into one collection; summoned highly learned men from all directions; selected the more experienced priests in the Mozarabic rite; and, having enriched them with resources, finally committed the Breviary according to the rule of Saint Isidore to the press in the year 1502.

But, lest we overstep the bounds of proper order, we shall first discuss the etymology of this holy office, and afterward matters pertaining to its antiquity.

## [Col. 0010A]

The etymology of the Mozarabic office is therefore used according to the designations of the nations among whom the Spaniards lived. In truth, in chronological order, the rite—although it was varied according to the changes of time and the ordinances of prelates—should first be called Roman and Hispanic, descending by tradition from Saints Peter and Paul’s disciples, the first founders and bishops of the Church of Spain: Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Indaletius, Hesychius, Euphrasius, Secundus, and Caecilius. Arriving at the shores of our Hesperia, they illumined it with the light of faith. It was then called Gothic, after Reccared, king of the Goths, converted to the Catholic faith and after the public renunciation of the Arian heresy in the First Council of Toledo.

## [Col. 0010B]

When Leander and his brother Isidore discovered that many things in the sacred liturgy and office had been deformed, corrupted, and twisted by the treachery of the Arians—for it is unbelievable that, from the time of Athaulf to Reccared, while Arian errors prevailed and Catholic bishops were in exile, numerous faults did not creep into the sacred autographs—they resolved to purge them of errors, restore them to greater purity, and arrange them in a better order. For this reason Leander and Isidore wrote about the divine offices, and nearly the entire purpose of the Fourth Council of Toledo, presided over by Saint Isidore, was to establish the order of the sacrifice of the Mass and of the divine offices throughout Spain and Gaul, and to restore the disfigured face to its former condition.

## [Col. 0010C]

Because of the great labors endured and the prolonged studies of Saint Isidore, the rite quite properly began to be called Isidorian: the Breviary and office according to the rule of the most blessed Isidore—that is, according to the canons of the Fourth Council of Toledo, which he himself had chiefly prepared, as president of the council and vicar of the Apostolic See, through his regulation of ecclesiastical rite and discipline, and as the most radiant star of the whole world.

After our Spain had been miserably occupied by the Moors, and Christians had become intermingled with the Arabs in food, clothing, and frequently in marriage, they entered into a peace treaty and obtained certain churches from the Moorish kings, while retaining their Catholic rites. The Missal and office were called Mozarabic.

## [Col. 0010D]

Who, even with bleary eyes, does not see that for nearly four hundred years of Arab rule, sacred rites were repeatedly celebrated secretly by Christians in the city of Toledo, often without a prelate or bishop? Who would not marvel that this rite did not perish utterly during that period, when the strength of the royal priesthood had failed? And if on some occasions, furtively and secretly, or after the Christians had paid the Saracens a great price, a bishop of this see of Toledo was chosen, it was still impossible—while the schools were closed and barbarism cast its shadow over all—to find a more learned or holier man in a condition of lost freedom, with preaching and teaching forbidden.

## [Col. 0011A]

At last the long-desired day dawned when the illustrious Alfonso VI captured Toledo and brought it under his authority, beginning with the sacred places. The Mezquita, formerly a mosque, was made into a sacred basilica. He summoned from Gaul men highly learned and deeply religious, so that he might raise them to episcopal thrones. He brought Cluniac monks—then at the height of their flourishing—to the canonries and dignities of the Church of Toledo. He appointed Bernard bishop of Toledo, Saint Peter bishop of Osma, another Bernard bishop of Sigüenza, and Saint Gerald bishop of Braga.

## [Col. 0011B]

From this time the Mozarabic office was called Toledan, because the kings of Castile and León began to reside at Toledo and to magnify the city and its church, on account of its secure location and its more fortified and easier access to the other towns occupied by the Moors and awaiting conquest. From that time onward, the small city, fortified by its position, was called a royal city.

From the time of Alfonso VI until the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, the kings of Castile could not enjoy quiet and peace; they moved from place to place, accustomed to war, and devotedly concerned with driving the Moors from all Spain. It was not possible to dispel the darkness of ignorance completely until, after the city of Granada had been conquered, the Catholic monarchs entrusted the task of putting affairs in better order to their outstanding counselors, the great Cardinals Pedro González de Mendoza—after whose death—Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros.

## [Col. 0011C]

These most illustrious lights of the Church took care to establish universities, colleges, hospitals, orphanages, cathedrals, and collegiate churches in Spain and in the Indies, and they left to posterity, at their own expense, certain excellent pious monuments worthy of imitation.

Cardinal Ximénez, like a resourceful bee, promptly selected the Sacred Bible, the Isidorian Missal, and the Isidorian office, so that they might be committed as quickly as possible to the press, recently introduced into Spain. For he judged that nothing was more useful, more welcome, or more beneficial to religion than to provide everyone with sacred books made more vigorous and pure.

## [Col. 0011D]

In the edition of the Isidorian Missal and Breviary, this distinguished man in no way intended to detract from the authority of the ancient Roman rite; rather, he intended to exalt it. For when this correction is compared with the ancient Gothic rite, it is clearly demonstrated that the Church, the Bride of Christ, has always and everywhere been one, united by the same Spirit, seamless—not torn apart by heretics, divided into parts, parceled out, and rent by them from top to bottom.

Although the same manner, order, and eloquence of Latin speech do not appear in all the prayers, nevertheless in the Gothic exemplars an unembellished idiom shines forth, not polished by art but redolent of antiquity. For that reason it is not so tightly bound by the rules of grammar, as may be seen in one or another passage of our edition. Otherwise, out of respect for the venerable age of the codex, we have left these features untouched.

## [Col. 0012A]

For the convenience of readers, especially those reciting the text, we have marked every word with its proper accent. In the Roman Missal and Breviary, however, everything is sufficiently well arranged, polished, purged of many errors, and improved through the vigilance of the most illustrious Cardinals Baronius, Bellarmine, and others. The hymns of Saint Ambrose and the other Fathers were reduced to better melody and meter and adapted to their proper places, so that they would retain their sense and not depart from the Latin orators and poets.

So much for the names given to this holy office.

Among the matters relating to the antiquity of the Gothic-Hispanic liturgy, the version claims the first place. The old Italic version was held in such high regard by the ancients and moderns that Saint Augustine did not hesitate to assert that it should be preferred to the other translations, because it adheres more closely to the words while preserving clarity of meaning. The Mozarabic priests use this version above all.

Here it is worth knowing that, so that the memory of the ancient Gothic-Hispanic rite might not perish, the aforementioned Ximénez commissioned the edition of the Breviary to Dr. Alfonso Ortiz, a canon of Toledo, who confesses in the dedication of the work:

“The nocturnal and likewise the diurnal offices, though issued with distinguished dignity, were difficult in respect of understanding and correction, and were revised through long and laborious study. Previously, nearly all of them had lain confused and unknown in old books, even among learned men. But through the expense and labor of the Cardinal, each was restored to its proper place, distinguished by type and punctuation, and clarified in words and sentences. The Isidorian offices, long endangered by age and worn away by antiquity, may now be read without difficulty by future generations.”

## [Col. 0012C]

Flaminius Nobilius, Morinus, Joannes Martianaeus, Thomas Hetarneus, Faber Stapulensis, Josephus Maria Caro, Cardinal Thomasius, and Petrus Sabatier afterward undertook the task of publishing the sacred codices. Sabatier also reviewed the others and rightly extolled Blanchini. From these last two distinguished authors, we have drawn whatever we found especially useful for our edition of the Gothic Breviary—not changing the appearance of the rite, but merely correcting it—by collating the readings with the Vatican, Veronese, Corbie, and Paris codices, those of Saint-Germain, and others.

## [Col. 0012D]

The edition of the old Italic version prepared by Petrus Sabatier with great labor served us so well that, guided by it, we did not grope blindly or stumble. For we found scarcely a word written in our Psalter that is not read elsewhere in the manuscripts, especially in the Gothic Bibles of Toledo and in Saint Augustine. Thus a safe path was open to us for correcting our Breviary: whenever a typographical error was evident, or whenever we happened to hesitate over the meaning of some word, we were strengthened by the agreement of other ancient readings.

How marvelous is the manifold grace of God! How marvelous is the sevenfold gift of the Paraclete Spirit, and the manifold gift of tongues, who has deigned, from the very substance of the sacred text, without substantial alteration of its meaning, to preserve for the Church so many translations not rejected by her, and the deposit of faith in so many kinds of language, in the Gothic manuscripts of the Vatican, Spain, and Gaul, preserved sound and whole for us to this day!

## [Col. 0013A]

But lest freedom to wander be indiscriminately granted to the faithful, and at the same time the liberty of heretics be restrained, the sacred Council of Trent removed from private persons the right of judgment in discerning sacred matters. From all the versions and editions of the Sacred Bible it selected the Vulgate, preferred it to the others, and declared it authentic, so that in a matter of such gravity laymen and women would not be made judges.

It did not, however, despise certain other versions, especially the Italic. Indeed, so that its antiquity and truth might become known, in the Roman office at Matins the psalm, or invitatory, **Come, let us rejoice in the Lord**, is recited almost word for word according to the old Italic version, the Vulgate being retained only on the day of the Epiphany of the Lord. Gregory the Great used both translations, sometimes the new and sometimes the old.

In the Introit of the Masses, look at the Graduals and Tracts of the Roman Missal itself. Verses according to the old Italic version, which the Gothic-Hispanic Psalter uses, are found throughout. For example, in the Introit of Septuagesima Sunday these words are recited: “The groans of death surrounded me,” rather than “the pain,” according to the Vulgate. In the common of martyrs during Paschaltide, Psalm 134 reads: “He will comfort his servants”; according to the Vulgate, “he will plead for them.”

## [Col. 0013C]

Lest we seem to exalt the version of the Isidorian Psalter excessively and assert on our own authority that it is extremely similar to the old Italic version, which, as stated, Augustine praises so highly, we shall cite several passages.

In Psalm XLVII, the Vulgate reads *odientes* (“those hating”), while the Isidorian Psalter has *odio habentes* (“having hatred”), just as Saint Augustine reads it.

In Psalm XVIII:3, both the Vulgate and other versions have *eructat*, whereas the old Italic version reads *eructuat*, as also in Augustine. Moreover, in verse 14 of the same psalm the Vulgate has *Si mei non fuerint dominati* (“If they shall not have ruled over me”); the Isidorian Psalter has *dominata*, as Augustine does.

In Psalm XX:3, the Vulgate and certain other versions read *desiderium cordis* (“the desire of the heart”), but the Mozarabic Psalter has *animae* (“of the soul”), as in Augustine. The Roman Church also repeats *animae* several times in the common of one martyr.

## [Col. 0013D]

According to the Vulgate, one hundred and fifty psalms of David, or of his disciples, are counted. Nevertheless, in our Isidorian Psalter and in the old Italic version, Psalm 151 is added, beginning: “I was small among my brothers and younger in my father’s house, etc.” It bears this heading:

“This psalm was specially written by David, outside the number, when he fought alone against Goliath.”

And if you compare not merely the heading but the words of the psalm, you will undoubtedly find the same text in the old Italic version—nowhere in the Vulgate edition or the others.

Moreover, examine carefully Psalm 118, **Blessed are the undefiled in the way**, and you will find so many marks of antiquity and so many numbers of annotation written in Hebrew, Roman, and ancient Hispanic letters that no doubt remains. It begins with the Hebrew letter **Aleph**; the Roman numeral I follows, and another Hispanic numeral is added. All signify the same thing, namely the first number. Then the beginning of the mystical meaning is indicated, and so the entire psalm is successively divided into sections of eight verses.

In the Vulgate only the Hebrew letters are appended, and those other letters added in our Psalter breathe the fragrance of antiquity.

In Psalm 95:8, these words are read in our codex: “Say among the nations: The Lord has reigned from the wood.” They are highly commended by Justin, Tertullian, and other Fathers, and are woven by Fortunatus into the hymn **The banners of the King advance**, in this form:

> The things are fulfilled that David  
> sang in faithful song,  
> saying among the nations:  
> God reigned from the wood.

Yet they are not found in the Vulgate, though they do appear in the old Italic version and in our Psalter.

## [Col. 0014A]

The learned reader may wish to know by whom and in what century this manuscript Psalter was written. In order not to overstep the bounds of sound judgment in clarifying both matters, we assert that the codex contains three parts: the Psalter, canticles, and hymns.

In the acrostic preface to the hymns, at the beginning of each hexameter, letters are read which produce the words: **“Mauricus, at the request of Veranianus, published it”**—the spelling of the manuscript is *edidyt*. From this it clearly appears that the copyist was a certain Mauricus, acting at Veranianus’s request or command. The identity of both the one giving the command and the one carrying it out is unknown to us, and there is no room for conjecture, since none of the councils of Toledo mentions a Bishop Veranianus.

Although Mauritius, bishop of Oretum, and Vera of Tarragona signed the councils of Toledo, no conclusion can be drawn from this; we may rely only on the signs of the writing.

In the canticles, the superscription of the prophets will seem reversed to you: Jeremiah appears for Nehemiah, Zechariah for Azariah, Jeremiah for Micah, Isaiah for Jeremiah, and Hosea. This could have happened partly through the copyist’s fault and partly for other reasons.

## [Col. 0014D]

And lest you raise your eyebrows, a similar example immediately occurs in our Vulgate. For in Matthew 27:9 these words—“They took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, etc.”—are attributed as words spoken by the prophet Jeremiah, with the statement: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah,” although it is certain that they were spoken not by Jeremiah but by Zechariah.

Further, in Mark 1:2 the words “Behold, I send my angel before your face” are attributed “according to the prophet Isaiah,” although they are truly from Malachi.

To unravel these and other difficulties, commentators adopt various explanations. But for our purpose the opinion of Saint Jerome is more agreeable. In Book II of his Commentary on Amos, chapter 5, he says:

> “In all the Holy Scriptures it must be observed that the apostles and apostolic men, when presenting testimonies from the Old Testament, consider not the words but the sense.”

## [Col. 0015A]

From this it follows that the Hispanic Church, in its version of the Sacred Bible, adheres in many respects to the old Italic version mentioned by Saint Augustine. Clement VIII bears witness that, in the Roman Missal and Breviary, several verses were also inserted according to that same version, and not according to the other versions current at that time. In the words prefixed to the bull of the Roman Missal, he says:

> “Although he [Pius V] had most strictly guarded against its being either added to or diminished in any way, by imposing many penalties, nevertheless, as time passed, the temerity and boldness of printers and others caused many errors to creep into the Missals printed in these recent years. Through these errors that most ancient version of the Sacred Bible, which was held in honor in the Church even before the time of Saint Jerome, and from which almost all the Introits of the Masses, together with the Graduals and Offertories, were taken, was entirely removed … The pretext for this seems to have been the desire to restore everything according to the prescription of the Vulgate edition of the Sacred Bible.”

Although Jerome must be considered the greatest teacher in the exposition of the Sacred Scriptures, the authority of Augustine has always been held in great weight in the Latin Church. Nor is it unknown to the learned that the Hispanic Church kept his works before its eyes, both because of the proximity of the regions and because of the frequent exchange of letters and the communication between African and Hispanic bishops.

## [Col. 0015C]

Canticle 23 in our Psalter is entitled **The Canticle of Tobit**, not **of Tobias**. Saint Augustine does the same, always calling the elder **Tobit** and the younger **Tobias**.

Saint Leander was exceedingly dear and closely joined in friendship to Saint Gregory the Great, as was Saint Isidore. Clear evidence of this is the fact that Pope Gregory dedicated his commentaries on Job to Leander, addressing him in words full of love and reverence.

Who, then, in his right mind would suppose that these holy doctors, sharing the same purpose, did not consult one another concerning the sacred versions and the books by which the Catholic faith might be supported and the Gothic people, recently converted to the faith, established in it?

Let someone else produce a similar example of a dedication by a supreme pontiff and great Doctor of the Church; let him bring forward other words filled with such benevolence as those of Gregory to Leander, from Book IV, Letter 46 of the *Register*:

> “With what ardor I long to see you, because you love me greatly, you may read in the tablets of your heart. But because I cannot see you, separated as you are by so great a distance of lands, I have done the one thing that charity toward you dictated to me: I have sent to Your Holiness, through our common son, the presbyter Probinus, the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, which I wrote at the beginning of my episcopate, and the books which you know I completed some time ago as a commentary on blessed Job.”

And at the end of the letter, excusing himself for its brevity, he adds these words, worthy of gold and cedar, addressing the same man:

> “The brevity of my letter itself makes my charity toward you known, since I speak little to the one whom I love more than all.”

Among the Fathers of the Church, where has a closer bond of friendship ever been read?

## [Col. 0016A]

Although Isidore was not Gregory’s disciple, he was highly esteemed by that same supreme pontiff. Gregory not only confirmed Isidore’s election by apostolic authority and adorned the elected bishop with the sacred pallium, but also appointed him his vicar throughout Spain.

Leo IV held no lower opinion of him. Writing to the bishops of Britain, he asserts that the sayings of Isidore, like those of Jerome and Augustine, should be retained when an unusual matter arises that cannot be settled by the canons.

Isidore’s fame eventually grew so great that, scarcely sixteen years after his death, with the Synod of Toledo—attended by fifty-two bishops—applauding and Saint Ildephonsus himself giving his support, he deserved to be called **the distinguished Doctor**, **the latest glory of the Catholic Church**, **the most learned man at the end of the ages**, and one whose name should be uttered with reverence.

## [Col. 0016B]

From what has been said up to this point, anyone may readily infer how many flowers these sacred doctors gathered from the Roman Church and its rite, since the way was open to them for sending messengers, and the supreme pontiffs strongly favored them in their successful undertakings.

I am no longer surprised that the Psalter according to the old Italic version, which the Fathers of Spain used, is recited to this day in the chapel of the supreme pontiff, and likewise in Venice in the major church of Saint Mark. For the Hispanic Fathers were moved by the same Spirit, guided by the same apostolic discipline, and borrowed from the See of Saint Peter what they lacked. It is the same version that Saint Gregory calls the old Vulgate, or translation, and that Saint Augustine calls the Italic.

So much for the version of this holy office.

Now I shall demonstrate the antiquity of the Gothic-Hispanic liturgy: first from the antiquity of the codices; second from its founders or compilers; and finally from the marks of the chant appended to the text called Eugenian.

## [Col. 0016C]

The pitiable and lamentable devastation of Spain wrought by the Saracens did not abolish the memory of the Hispanic Fathers. Although the pagans sought to consign their writings to complete oblivion—some erased, some filled with errors and fables, some lost, some defiled, and finally some handed over to the flames—nevertheless, after the Moors had been expelled, the honor due to such great Fathers was restored through the work and diligence of Cardinals Ximénez, Loaysa, and Aguirre, in the edition of the rite and of the Councils of Toledo.

## [Col. 0016D]

If some error has crept into the manuscript codices, the fault must be attributed to the copyists, not the authors. For if today, while the art of printing flourishes, errors and faults are found everywhere in books, what wonder if, at the beginning of the invention, the Isidorian Missal and Breviary were filled with very many errors?

Nor do we have such confidence in our own labor that we think a similar fate could not befall us in some respect. For on page 59 the name of Saint Thomas of Canterbury is found, as it appears in the edition of Don Ortiz. It was inserted there—or rather slipped in—without our awareness.

## [Col. 0017A]

The Gothic codices that we examined, worn out by age, broken, torn, and with their letters nearly erased and consumed, do not nourish the bookworms, for they are often handled. But moth and rust corrode and destroy not only parchments, papyri, and wood, but even marble.

Many native and foreign authors testify without hesitation that the Gothic manuscripts—the autographs from Complutum that served for printing the Isidorian Missal and Breviary—are preserved. While we were in that aforementioned city, we searched for them carefully and eagerly, but waited in vain. Nor, according to Master Flórez, could they have been there, for the Missal and Breviary were printed at Toledo, and therefore the autographs ought to have been preserved there.

## [Col. 0017B]

Grieved at being deprived of such a desire, we returned to the Library of our Holy Church of Toledo, where we fulfilled our hopes to some extent.

In it are found eight Gothic manuscript codices. One contains, besides seven Masses believed to have been composed by Saint Ildephonsus with musical notation, the offices of the Nativity, Circumcision, and Apparition of the Lord, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, and the office of John the Apostle and Evangelist.

Another contains the complete office of Lent up to, but excluding, Palm Sunday.

Another contains, besides some Masses, the office of Holy Week through Easter inclusively, together with certain offices of the saints.

Another contains the offices of the saints throughout the year.

Another contains the Epistles and Gospels for the entire year.

Another contains the Masses of the saints throughout the year.

Finally, another contains the complete Psalter with canticles and hymns.

Besides these codices, the aforementioned library preserves a Gothic Bible that belonged during the time of Muslim captivity to Servandus, bishop of Astigi. It later belonged to John, bishop of Carthage and Córdoba, who gave it to the Church of Seville in the Spanish era 1026, in the year of Christ 988.

## [Col. 0017C]

Nevertheless, I do not intend to paint the face of this very ancient codex with cosmetic coloring, nor to conceal what will become evident to the keenest eyes of the learned.

We recognize some difference, although slight, in the alteration of certain words between the Isidorian Breviary printed by Cardinal Ximénez and the aforementioned manuscript codices. Accordingly, it may be conjectured either that Alfonso Ortiz, canon of Toledo, had other autographs before his eyes, now lost, or that Alfonso himself, protected by the authority of Cardinal Ximénez, when troubled by obscure passages of the Psalms, had recourse to the Vulgate or another version and added certain words in accordance with it.

## [Col. 0017D]

Yet both this matter itself and the feasts and saints’ offices added to the Mozarabic rite provided an opening for its attackers. Since it is as clear as midday that the feast of Corpus Christi was composed after the errors of Berengarius, and since Saints Thomas of Canterbury, Francis, and others whose memory is celebrated throughout the year in the Mozarabic Breviary flourished many centuries after Saint Isidore of Seville, they seize upon this as an opportunity to detract from the authority of the Breviary.

But they do so most unjustly, as the aforementioned Reverend Father Enrique Flórez proves and establishes by many arguments.

The Roman Missal and Breviary, corrected by the supreme pontiffs Pius V, Clement VIII, and Urban VIII, did not cease to be Roman, derived from the most ancient exemplars and descending from the tradition of the apostles, because certain feasts were added—feasts that had not been celebrated in the first centuries—or because saints of our own age, or of the immediately preceding ages, were entered in the catalogue of the blessed, for whom a proper Mass and office are recited.

## [Col. 0018A]

No one may therefore rightly conjecture that its antiquity is diminished by such an increase in the Church and by the greater extension of the rite.

## [Col. 0018B]

In the same way, the Hispanic Missal and Breviary did not lose that designation after the Gothic people were converted to our Catholic faith. For although Leander, Isidore, Ildephonsus, Eugenius, and Julian enlarged it, corrected it, and brought it into better form, they did not alter the appearance of the earlier rite; rather, they made it more beautiful and dignified.

A wise son does not overshadow his father’s glory, nor does a disciple’s greater insight obscure the teacher’s faith. The works of God’s servants are first planted; afterward irrigation is poured upon them until they take root and grow together, and finally are made more pleasing and useful by their abundant fruits.

For the higher a building rises, the deeper its foundation is sunk at the beginning. The rubble is first hidden in the bowels of the earth, so that the structure may afterward be raised more securely and with a more beautiful appearance.

## [Col. 0018C]

The holy disciples of the apostles, dispersed through the four quarters of the world, destroyed idolatry and sowed the Catholic faith; they established order and office in divine worship. Transmitting the ministry and power of their apostleship to their successors in the episcopal sees, they began to multiply and increase the Hispanic Church day by day.

The bishops ordered sacred matters, strove to preserve the traditions of their ancestors, and watered the hearts of the faithful, even though the savagery of pagan emperors opposed them, until, peace having been restored to the Church, they were permitted to perform the sacred rites openly.

Behold the succession of the apostles! Behold the order descending from the apostles in the divine offices! Behold, finally, this western region of Spain irradiated by the light of faith and adorned by the beauty of the rite.

Lest anyone imagine that the Spaniards in these earliest centuries of the Church should be counted among barbarians, let him consider, I beg, the condition in which the other regions of the world remained with respect to religion, once it had been expanded and ordered, when Saint Sylvester summoned from Spain the great Hosius of Córdoba to preside in his name at the first ecumenical Council of Nicaea. There the rule of faith to be presented to all and the first foundations of ecclesiastical discipline had to be laid. That great man Hosius was chosen by the great Constantine to enlighten the others at Nicaea, Sardica, Rome, and other councils, and in catechesis; so that everyone marveled at his wisdom and, with one voice, responded when the canons were promulgated: “Hosius said; Hosius replied.” Born in Spain, trained in secular letters and instructed in the sacred liturgy, he could not rightly extend and order the sacred rite throughout the world if he had been negligent in his own region and Church and did not know how to govern his own household.

Whoever still hesitates should read through the words of Athanasius in his *History of the Arians to the Monks*, which I am pleased to quote. After such and so many crimes, the impious Arians, thinking that they had accomplished nothing so long as the great Hosius had not experienced their malignity, attempted to extend their fury to so venerable an old man. They showed no reverence for the father of bishops, no respect for a confessing man, and did not blush before the length of his episcopate, in which he had spent more than sixty years; but, setting aside and despising everything else, they cared only for heresy—men, in truth, who neither fear God nor reverence human beings. Accordingly, they approached Constantius and addressed him in these words:

“We have left nothing undone. We have sent the Roman bishop into exile, and before him many other bishops; we have filled every place with terror. Yet all your great achievements will profit us nothing, and nothing has yet been rightly accomplished by us, so long as Hosius remains unharmed. For while he remains among his own people, they all remain in their Churches; by his word and faith he can draw everyone against us. He is accustomed to preside over synods, and everywhere all obey his letters. He promulgated the Nicene faith and everywhere exposed the Arians as heretics. If he remains, therefore, the exile of the others will have been useless; for our heresy must soon be removed from the midst of us. Begin, then, to persecute him also, and do not spare the man, however advanced in age he may be; for our heresy does not know how to revere even the gray hair of old men.”

The Catholic teaching of Hosius was transmitted to the bishops of Spain as though by hereditary right: from Hosius, who died in the year 356, to Saint Leander; from Leander to Isidore; from Isidore to Helladius; from him to Ildephonsus and Eugenius; from the Eugeniuses to Julian II, who, at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, by order of Leo II, Roman pontiff, approved the acts of the Sixth General Council. When Benedict, Leo’s successor, had read those words of Julian of Toledo in his discussion of the Trinity—namely, that “wisdom proceeds from wisdom” and “will from will,” together with other statements by which he asserted that Christ the Lord consisted of three substances—which Benedict believed deviated from the common judgment of the Catholic Church, Julian published an *Apologeticus* at the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in defense of these propositions. Sent to Rome, it was held in high esteem and ordered to be read by all, while the pope exclaimed: “Your praise, O God, reaches to the ends of the earth.” For Julian and the other Spanish Fathers expressed these statements in a true and Catholic sense, as can be seen in the acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo apud Cardinal Aguirre, who also includes Julian’s apology. In it the sharpness of his intellect and his profound understanding of the dogmas of the faith shine forth. To this may be added the Council of Elvira, convened at the beginning of the fourth century, from which the universal Church derived many things.

[Col. 0020A] If some overly scrupulous person, after comparing the Mozarabic Breviary printed by Cardinal Ximenes with the Breviary presently reissued by us, notices a slight variation in certain words, let him not blame the author but the copyist; let him not accuse Alfonso Ortiz, but show indulgence toward the printers. Let him firmly believe that, formerly, because of the lack of a press, the sacred manuscripts were preserved in each individual Mozarabic parish of Toledo, and that Ortiz recognized some difference. Pressed by this anxiety, as we have already said, and enveloped in darkness, he corrected certain words according to the Vulgate, fearing that, by using an unfamiliar form of a word or an unusual transposition, he might appear to employ an unaccustomed version and depart from the straight path.

Let the reader therefore attribute whatever variation may now appear to the fault of copyists, in view of the public edition of the old Italian version according to the Vatican, Saint-Germain, Corbie, Queen Christina of Sweden, and other manuscripts, published by Pierre Sabatier. No difference in substance is to be supposed; rather, there is a marvelous agreement in meaning with some discrepancy in wording. Thus, if the manuscript Psalter preserved in the library of the Holy Church of Toledo is carefully examined, scarcely a word will be found in it that has not been transcribed in one of the aforementioned codices or in the text read by Saint Augustine.

The authority of the Isidorian Breviary, published by the great cardinal, is therefore not obscured by the addition of certain saints who flourished after the Saracens had been expelled from Spain. For they have neither a proper office, readings, responsories, nor prayers; everything is said from the common office, as Father Enrique Flórez has already noted in his dissertation on the Mozarabic office. Since the office is thus, for the most part, according to the common Gothic form, nothing was added except the names of the saints, apart from certain feasts.

Francisco de Pisa published a fragment of the Gothic-Mozarabic Calendar preserved in the Toledo library, containing only the months of January and February. But since it appears truncated and defective, and since it assigns to January 28 the feast of Saint Serena, virgin and martyr—who is found neither in our manuscript codices nor in any martyrology as a virgin—it is consequently of doubtful reliability. Moreover, on February 1 the manuscript contains this inscription: “The Beginning of February among the Egyptians.” This feast is nowhere found in our codices, although we know for certain that the beginning of February was sanctified among them for the destruction of idolatry, and that at the beginning of that month the feast of the Amburbials was customarily celebrated by the pagans. In its place there later succeeded the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary, to abolish the memory of the abduction of Proserpina by Pluto, as is demonstrated from Innocent III, Rabanus Maurus, and others, and explicitly asserted by Saint Ildephonsus in his sermon on the Purification.

Another suspicion against the aforesaid fragment arises from its silence concerning the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary, although elsewhere it assigns the death of Saint Ildephonsus, whose office is nowhere mentioned in the Gothic rite; moreover, that very saint delivered a sermon to the people on the Purification.

In the middle of certain psalms the word *Diapsalma* is inserted. It is rarely found in the Isidorian Breviary printed by Cardinal Ximenes, but if one follows the autograph, it is encountered many times. It denotes a separation between one verse and another of the same psalm. It therefore served to mark a pause in psalmody and to regulate the singing in accordance with the musical signs.

In the middle of other psalms the following sign is inserted, signifying the same thing as “repeat.” For the sign consists of all its letters joined together. The singers were required to repeat an antiphon derived from the words of the psalm itself. This occurred not in shorter but in longer psalms, so that they might enjoy a certain rest during the recitation and that the monotony might be relieved by variety in the singing.

We shall gladly add other proofs to indicate the antiquity of our rite. In the codex called the Aemilianus, preserved in the royal monastery of El Escorial and written before the year 1078, bearing the title “Concerning the Apostolic Mass Introduced into Spain, by Julian and Felix,” it is asserted in §1 that the seven apostolic men—Torquatus, Ctesiphon, and the others mentioned—received the priesthood from the holy apostles Peter and Paul and began to preach in the cities of Spain concerning the beginning of immortal life. A little later it adds:

“And thus, just as they received the teaching of the Mass from the apostles, they handed it on throughout Spain after ordaining bishops.”

Section 2 concerns the office of the Spanish Church, praised and approved at Rome in the time of Pope John, while Charles was king of the Franks and Ordoño king in the city of León. When the priest Zanellus had been sent by the aforesaid supreme pontiff John to investigate the condition of ecclesiastical religion there and faithfully report what he had discovered to the Apostolic See, he diligently carried out the task entrusted to him. He examined the entire order of the ecclesiastical office and the rule of consecration, read the canons and all the sacramental books, and, finding everything fortified by the Catholic faith, rejoiced. He reported to Pope John and to the entire assembly of the Roman Church what he had found. When the lord pope and the whole Roman Church heard this, they gave thanks to God, praised and confirmed the office of the Spanish Church, and added only this: that thereafter the secret prayers of the Mass should henceforth be celebrated according to the custom of the Apostolic Church.

[Col. 0021D] The supreme pontiff Gregory VII, writing to Alfonso VI, king of León, to Sancho V of Navarre, and to the bishops subject to them, addresses them at the beginning of his letter as follows:

“Since the blessed apostle Paul indicates that he went to Spain, and since afterward seven bishops were sent from the city of Rome by the apostles Peter and Paul to instruct the peoples of Spain—men who, after destroying idolatry, established Christianity, planted religion, displayed the order and office of divine worship, and dedicated the Churches with their own blood—your diligence should not be unaware of this. How great an agreement Spain had with the city of Rome in religion and in the order of divine worship is sufficiently clear.”

He then exhorts them to embrace the Roman rite in Spain. Although he states that the Spanish office was polluted by the madness of the Priscillianists, corrupted by the perfidy of the Arians, and finally diminished by the invading Saracens, these words in no way overturn what was said earlier. For through the care of the holy Isidore, Ildephonsus, Julian, and the other Fathers of Spain, the office was cleansed of every stain, if any had been present, and restored to its integrity and purity, as Felix testifies when speaking of Saint Julian. The Roman office of this saint, drawn from the same Felix, agrees with him.

[Col. 0022B] The Roman pontiffs themselves, later becoming more certain of the office’s sincerity, confirmed it by repeated diplomas. In 1508 Julius II, at the request of Cardinal Ximenes, strengthened the office in these words:

“Most ancient and of great devotion … We therefore, who, in fulfillment of our pastoral office, sincerely desire the increase of divine worship … approve and confirm, by apostolic authority and by the tenor of these presents, everything and each individual matter contained in the aforesaid letters.”

In 1512 he issued another bull supporting the Mozarabic office. This approval by the Apostolic See, so explicit and precise—as Pinius says—ought to close everyone’s mouth, so that after it no one would dare even to murmur against the restored use of the Mozarabic office and the foundation of its ministers. For this reason Paul III desired someone to rival the work of Ximenes by publishing the sacred Mozarabic volumes anew; and we are taking care to fulfill his wish.

In the *Acts of the Saints*, volume VI for July, in the preliminary treatise, no. 10, concerning the blessed apostle James, these words are added:

“It follows that that apostle designated the sacred rites of the liturgy there; indeed, insofar as the time available for remembrance permitted, he handed on and confirmed what he had received from Saint Peter concerning the matter in question.”

And in the same place, no. 6:

“Saint Paul also perhaps devoted his efforts to that end.”

The same thing is plainly established by the decretal of Innocent I.

That distinguished doctor himself, from whom the present office, as we have said, received its name, says in Book II of the *Office*, chapter 15:

“The order of the Mass and of the prayers by which the sacrifices offered to God are consecrated was first instituted by Saint Peter; the whole world celebrates it in one and the same manner.”

Consider, I beg, Isidore’s judgment. If in his time the whole world celebrated the sacred liturgy in one and the same manner, then without doubt the Fathers of Spain celebrated the sacrifice according to the ancient Roman order, differing in nothing from the Roman See; otherwise he would not have called it “one and the same manner.” O pitiable greed of the Arabs, which not only almost consumed certain most precious remnants of the sacred codices but also left others, preserved by God’s gift, enveloped in great darkness! By striving to bury the sacred basilicas, devastate them, depopulate the cities, and erase the memory of our rite, you have supplied modern critics with material for doubt and dispute!

[Col. 0023A] Many of Isidore’s works certainly perished, but that savagery could not consume them all. The writings of Julian, bishop of Toledo, disappeared for the most part, but his apology for the three substances remained intact for posterity, as a demonstration of his orthodox teaching. Likewise, the works of Eugenius II, bishop of Toledo, in verse and prose; the letters of Montanus; and several other monuments of the Gothic Fathers before the invasion of the Moors sufficiently display their eloquence, their more fitting meaning, their uniformity in interpreting Scripture, and their reverence for the Apostolic See.

Even during the time of the Muslim captivity, some learned letters under excellent teachers, were instructed in the precepts of the faith, taught them publicly, and professed them before kings. This happened in the case of the blessed Eulogius, elected bishop of Toledo, who not only defended the steadfastness of the martyrs in his apology but also honored their acts in his *Memorial*. He did not fear the pagan fury, but sealed with his own blood what he believed in his heart unto righteousness and confessed with his mouth unto salvation.

Let us explain our position more clearly. We do not assert that the Gothic rite, during the first five centuries of the Church, was identical in every respect with the Roman rite in all sacred prayers. Rather, we maintain that in origin and substance—as Cardinal Bona indicates in Book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 7, no. 5—the sacrifice consisted of the same substantial parts, namely consecration, oblation, and reception, although the accidental order of the prayers changed over time both in Italy and in Spain.

Nor do we need to dwell on defending the opinion of Cajetan Cenni, who, speaking of the Mass celebrated in Spain in the time of Saint Isidore, says as follows in volume I, dissertation VII, no. 10:

“Clearly it was very similar to that which Saint Peter instituted. If it appears quite different from the ancient Roman rite, who does not know that Leo, Gelasius, and Gregory brought that rite to the form which exists today? The case is different with the Spanish rite: none of the sacramentaries of those three pontiffs knows it; rather, the Mass which our Hesperia received earlier from the Holy See, that is the Mass which it preserved.”

[Col. 0023D] Just as in nature birth comes first, growth afterward, and perfection last, so in the celebration of sacred things the original order was born from the Apostolic See, then grew, and finally reached perfection. According to Isidore, the Gothic rite is very similar to the Roman. In the passage cited above he says:

“There are seven prayers of the sacrifice commended by evangelical and apostolic teaching,”

and we see the same rite preserved today in the Mozarabic Mass. In the first, called the *Missa*, an admonition is given to the people; in the second, an invocation or supplication is made to God; in the third, inscribed *Post Nomina*, prayer is offered for those making the offering; in the fourth, prayer is made for peace and unity; in the fifth, a proclamation or offering is made for the gifts received; in the sixth, *Post Pridie*, conformity with the sacrament is expressed; and in the seventh, prayer is made in connection with the Lord’s Prayer.

On this basis, together with Cardinal Bona, we confidently judge that the rite in Africa and Gaul was similar to that called Mozarabic in Spain. With respect to Gaul, there is clear testimony in the letter of Charles the Bald, whose words the distinguished Mabillon quotes in his treatise on the liturgy. For after certain Spanish priests had celebrated the most holy sacrifice of the Mass in the king’s presence, at a time when the Gauls had embraced the Roman rite from the time of Pepin, the king testified that he had seen the rite of his ancestors.

[Col. 0024A] As for the canonical office, or Isidorian Breviary, there is no need to search through the inner chambers of the earlier centuries, nor to unroll archival chests to prove its unity and conformity with the very ancient Roman rite. It is composed of the same hours. If it adds the dawn, we clearly see that this was customary in the earliest centuries of the Church, when the faithful rose at the first light of dawn to offer God the first fruits of the light.

As regards its order, however, a variation introduced over time can be observed, partly deriving from the monks and partly intended to increase devotion—so that we might say that the sacred rite was enlarged and enriched—and adopted by the supreme pontiffs.

Since, therefore, we possess in the Isidorian Psalter a highly esteemed version of the old Italian text, and since at the end of every psalm it says, “Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” in accordance with article 14 of the Third Council of Toledo, in its profession of faith, and canon 15 of the Fourth Council, presided over by Saint Isidore, there is no room for doubt that it remained intact and without any substantial alteration down to the time of Cardinal Ximenes. Nor could this be changed by the feasts drawn by Cardinal Ximenes from the ancient Toledan rite, whose Missal was later printed by Cardinals Juan de Tavera and Martínez Silíceo, before the correction of Pius V.

The use of the psalms with singing at the beginning, and, when they were longer, with a pause sometimes around the middle—a pause they called *diapsalma*, as was said—belonged to the age of Saint Isidore, as the Psalter will show in the form in which it appears in the autograph published by us. The holy doctor himself demonstrates this in Book I, chapter 1, §1, of *On the Divine Offices*, concerning the psalms, in these words:

“Because of the carnal, not because of the spiritual, the custom of singing was instituted in the Church: so that, since they are not pierced by words, they may be moved by the sweetness of melody … for, according to Augustine, our minds are moved more religiously and ardently toward the flame of piety by those holy words themselves when they are sung than when they are not sung.”

And again Isidore says:

“All our emotions are aroused more strongly by the variety or novelty of sounds, through some hidden familiarity, when something is sung with a sweet and artful voice.”

[Col. 0024D] The holy doctor mentions hymns in the following section, listing their earliest composers: Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, distinguished for his eloquence, and Ambrose of Milan, whom he calls a man of great glory in Christ, a most celebrated doctor in the Church, and prolific in composing such poems. Hence, from his name, they are called Ambrosian hymns. Devotion to their fame was first observed in the Church of Milan and afterward throughout the Churches of the entire West.

Now, therefore, we ask the reader to turn his eyes to the hymns of the present Isidorian rite. He will discover that they are the same hymns which Saint Isidore reports as being recited. If others are found, they were composed by the Spanish Prudentius, who flourished in the fourth century.

In the hymn of Saint James only eleven apostles are enumerated, and the author—or, more probably, the copyist—passes over Judas Thaddaeus in silence. See the prologue to the exposition of the Apocalypse by Saint Beatus of Liébana, recently published by the Reverend Father Flórez, Book II. Do not immediately be alarmed; rather, marvel at its antiquity. Although Cardinal Ximenes supplied this omission in the body of the hymn by adding Saint Thaddaeus, and Father Flórez likewise noted in the margin the words “Judas Thaddaeus omitted,” nevertheless, if conjecture is permitted, you should attribute the matter to ignorance, excessive piety, and the fault of the copyist during the period of Muslim captivity, not to the author. The copyist, misled by error, feared where there was no fear that Saint Judas might be confused with the betrayer.

In the aforesaid Psalter, *mici* is always written for *mihi*, *macina* for *machina*; sometimes *b* appears for *v*, or conversely; *Josep* for *Joseph*, *Asap* for *Asaph*, *tropeum* for *trophaeum*, and many other similar forms occur, with the aspiration of the letter *h* omitted. This is an evident sign of Gothic pronunciation and writing. Their native tongue was guttural and had great difficulty becoming accustomed to refined Latin speech. For this reason, unskilled ancient copyists inserted the words mentioned above, as can be seen in other codices of the same period. So that they would not remain an obstacle for Mozarabic priests, these words were corrected in the aforesaid Psalter.

[Col. 0025C] Until now, all scholars have eagerly desired to know the solemnities or feasts of the saints celebrated by the Gothic Fathers. They could not extract them from the Breviary printed by Cardinal Ximenes, for, as we have said, it contains the feast of the Most Holy Body of Christ, instituted in the thirteenth century by Urban IV to abolish the error of Berengarius. It also contains, among the feasts throughout the year, many saints listed in the common office who had no office at all in the Gothic period; indeed, some flourished many centuries later.

Now, however, the feasts celebrated in the Gothic period—or shortly before the invasion of the Moors—are distinguished from our very ancient manuscript codices, and scholars can readily learn what they desired. For the hymns inserted in the body of the Breviary and after the canticles all agree with the antiquity of the rite; none has been omitted in the codex as it stands. To avoid the tedium of repetition, when hymns occur in the body of the Breviary, a reference is made to the proper feast. Although the edition of Cardinal Ximenes differs in certain words from our manuscript codex, the discrepancy is slight and is no just cause for correcting the aforesaid hymns.

[Col. 0025D] A significant argument for the antiquity of our codex arises from the number and order of the canonical hours to which the hymns are adapted; they present us with an image of the earlier centuries of the Church. At the end of our codex, therefore, one finds not only hymns for the morning hours and Lauds, but also hymns for the first nocturnal vigil, for cockcrow—which occurred around midnight—and for the crowing of the chicks, which occurred around the rising dawn. To distinguish this second time from the cockcrow at midnight, they called the hymn “the crowing of the chicks.”

In addition, they assigned other hours, so that they might spend the twelve hours of the day in sacred hymns, according to that saying of our Lord Jesus Christ: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” They also referred to the parable of the vineyard, for the cultivation of which laborers were hired not only at the ninth hour but also at the tenth and eleventh, so that the ministers of the Lord might meditate on his law day and night and devote themselves to divine worship.

For this reason, you will read hymns for cockcrow around midnight; for the crowing of the chicks around the beginning of the rising dawn; for Prime, when the star has risen and daylight has begun; for Terce, around the ninth hour of the day; for the fourth hour, around the tenth hour; for Sext, around the twelfth hour; for the seventh hour, around the second hour of Vespers; for None, around the third hour; for the tenth hour, around the fourth; for the eleventh, around the fifth; for the twelfth, around the sixth; and for Vespers, around sunset.

Before Compline a hymn was also recited with prayers. Finally, at Compline, before sleep and when prepared for bed, they sprinkled their dwellings with blessed water and prayed to God that the phantoms of the night might depart far away, that they might sleep in peace, that their bodies might not be polluted, and that they might awaken with Christ.

[Col. 0026C] Consider, I beg, this sacred distribution of day and night. Compare it with the canonical hours observed by the faithful after the sixth century. Examine the custom of the monks of the East, as well as the ancient constitutions of the monastery of Lérins and of others. When you see it in our Gothic rite, cast away all anxiety concerning its venerable antiquity.

The injuries of time may indeed have caused certain parchment leaves to perish; the savagery and barbarism of the Moors may have destroyed many Gothic monuments; the ignorance of copyists may have mingled errors into the Latin language. But none of these could abolish our golden manuscript codex, from which, as from a fingernail, the antiquity of our Isidorian rite may be inferred: a rite transcribed even during the period of Arab domination and still extant to the present day.

Some, deceived by error, have said that the councils of Toledo celebrated during the Gothic period were royal assemblies rather than councils. They rely on the following grounds: that an oath of fidelity was often sworn to elected kings; that matters concerning the government of the kingdom were frequently discussed with the king and nobles; that kings and magnates signed together with the Fathers; that the royal tome was presented before the beginning of the synod; and finally that a decree confirming the council was appended.

But none of these things is opposed to the sacred assemblies of the Gothic Fathers or to their sacred liturgy, especially since the Roman Church permitted the one hundred and seventy-six canons drawn from the Councils of Toledo and from Saint Isidore, collected by Gratian, to be publicly taught; it granted them its authority and made them its own. Moreover, it is not a novelty in the Church for public ordinances, made at the will of princes, to be mingled with sacred matters in the synods of the Fathers. These ordinances had a particular place in the elections of the Gothic kings, so that the other vassals, following the example of the bishops, might obey their princes more willingly and readily and openly and securely acknowledge that the election had been properly conducted. We see the same practice in the ancient pontificals and in the capitularies of Charlemagne.

[Col. 0027A] A clear proof of this matter was the harmony between priesthood and empire, such that statutes and sacred prayers joined both powers in a marvelous bond. Thus the hymns for the ordination and birthday of the king, for the departure of the army—intended to be sung on the days of the litanies until its return—and for various calamities are most ancient and proper to the Goths. No one who has read them will deny this. So that no opportunity for doubt might remain, we have printed them. Would that Alfonso Ortiz had done the same, so that every cloud of uncertainty might have disappeared.

Father Flórez has exerted himself greatly in defending the four verses of the hymn mentioning Bishop Cixila in connection with Saint Thyrsus. He assumes with certainty that they are found in the older Toledan manuscripts. Lest anyone be deceived in the future, we point out that in our manuscripts—the ones we so often mention—those words are nowhere found:

> This temple, Lord, Cixila founded;  
>   
> May he have a worthy lot here;  
>   
> With the foremost citizens may he sing songs in the rest,  
>   
> Rejoicing throughout all the everlasting ages.

Once freed from this difficulty, the reader needs no other testimony to establish the truth of our rite. Although Cardinal Baronius assigns this Saint Thyrsus to January 24, as can be seen in his notes on the martyrology for that day, nevertheless in our manuscript and in the Gothic office he occupies a place on January 28. On that day Saint Leucius the martyr, the companion of Saint Thyrsus in his passion, is also mentioned, as appears from the hymn.

Those who have studied the works of Saint Isidore will find there testimony to his wisdom, and every doubt concerning our rite and his comprehensive learning will vanish. He treated the liberal arts as a more learned modern writer might do, and the ecclesiastical offices according to the golden early centuries of Rome. As apostolic vicar he himself presided over the national Fourth Council of Toledo. In view of these distinguished achievements, it is incredible that the stream of his eloquence did not pour out upon all subjects, especially those concerning the ordering of the sacred liturgy and divine offices.

In the handwritten autograph before our eyes for the edition of this Breviary, unmistakable signs of this matter appear. We shall indicate some of them, so that the similarity of the others with the rite rightly and deservedly called Isidorian may be recognized. Thus, first, to mark a paragraph, so that one matter may be separated from matters connected with it, Saint Isidore uses the following sign, in chapter 20. It denotes a difference of discourse; and the very same sign can be found in our manuscript autograph marking the division of a treatise or placed before the beginning of the numbering of the psalms.

Another sign appears in the form of [figure], which he calls *Phietro*. It is placed to indicate a difficulty where there is some obscurity; and the same sign, with a slight modification, is sometimes found in our manuscript autograph.

Singing without a clef or lines, unfamiliar in the present age, appears in our autograph as consisting solely of musical points. According to Isidore, these were distinguished clearly and distinctly in the three parts of music: harmonic, rhythmic, and metric. As regards the harmonic, it produces in all who sing with their own voice a movement arising from inward feeling and ardor, and from movement it produces sound.

According to Isidore, *tone*—Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22—is the acute utterance of the voice, the difference and quantity of harmony, which consists in the accent or sustained quality of the voice. Musicians divided its kinds into fifteen parts, of which the hyperlydian is the last and highest, while the hypodorian is the lowest of all. Singing, therefore, is the inflection of the voice according to the rules laid down by Saint Isidore; for a direct sound is one thing, and sound precedes singing.

The holy doctor was not unaware of the difference between sweet and full voices. He defines with remarkable precision the acute, thin, high, hard, rough, blind, wine-toned, and perfect voice. The perfect voice is high, sweet, and clear: high, so that it may rise aloft; clear, so that it may fill the ears; and sweet, so that it may charm the minds of those who hear.

[Col. 0028C] Saint Isidore gives certain arithmetical rules for distinguishing musical numbers, which will delight anyone highly skilled in the art of music today. “You will seek numbers,” he says in the cited work, chapter 23, “according to music in this way. Having set down the extremes, for example 6 and 12, you see by how many units 12 exceeds 6; it is six units. You multiply by the square: six times six makes 36. You join the two original extremes, 6 and 12; together they make 18. You divide 36 by 18, and the result is a *dipondius* (two units). You join this with the smaller sum, namely 6; the result is 8, and this is the mean between 6 and 12. For 8 exceeds 6 by two units, that is, by one-third of six, and 8 is exceeded by 12 by four units, a third portion. Thus, by the same fraction by which one exceeds, one is exceeded.”

Why should we say more, if the way is open for readers to examine Isidore’s statements?

The agreement between the works of Saint Isidore and this Breviary of ours shines forth especially in the inscription of the reading from Ecclesiasticus. In the Breviary it bears this heading: “Reading from the Book of Ecclesiasticus of Solomon.” Since it is universally established that the book of Ecclesiasticus was composed by Jesus son of Sirach of Jerusalem, not by Solomon, a difficulty immediately arises: why is it identified in this way in the Breviary? Saint Isidore answers this in his *Book of Prologues to the Old Testament*, in the section “On Ecclesiasticus”:

“Because of the excessive similarity of meaning and equality of eloquence, it is prefaced under Solomon’s title.”

We shall not linger further in defending the antiquity of the Isidorian rite on the basis of the conformity visible in the Psalter according to the old Italian version, with certain words borrowed from Saint Jerome’s translation; the signs used for writing the characters; the singing and melody, a specimen of which we offer you; the similarity of the liturgy; the Gallican office published by Father Blanchini and illuminated by Pinius; especially the prayers of the Breviary, in which only slight diversity is observed between the Veronese codices and ours; and finally the simplicity of the words of the hymns of Ambrose and the other Fathers as they came from their authors themselves.

No sensible person will deny that Saint Ambrose, trained in more polished letters, was thoroughly acquainted with the precepts of grammar and poetry. When someone sees that the hymns composed by this most illustrious doctor are inelegant and not bound by meter, he should understand that this occurred for many reasons. First, because, as Augustine says of himself, Ambrose intended to preserve not so much rules as meanings. Second, because of the fault and negligence of copyists who, transferring texts from one person to another and increasing the errors, utterly disfigure and alter the author’s form and meaning. In later centuries it became impossible even to discern the aim of the discourse or conjecture its sense. Let prudent critics therefore attribute the fault to the ravages of the moths, the errors of notaries, the ignorance of translators, and the other defects of pen and press; and let them marvel that the texts have reached us at all in the form in which they survive.

Examples will make the matter clearer. The seventy translators, as they say, were placed separately from one another—whether in one location or in distant places—by Ptolemy Philadelphus, and translated the sacred books delivered to them into Greek, as though by a miracle. No one is unaware that the sacred books, so translated, were preserved in the imperial library with great care, skill, and diligence [Col. 0029C]; nor can one doubt the zeal of Jews and Christians in obtaining copies letter for letter. Yet afterward there arose in the East almost countless translations by Origen, Jerome, Aquila, Theodotion, and unknown translators, both rabbinical and Latin, so that the Council of Trent judged it necessary to restrain freedom of opinion and to declare the text according to the Vulgate authentic.

In our own time, interpreters and theologians debate whether the words, “And there are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit,” belong in the body of the First Epistle of Saint John, chapter V, or merely in a marginal note [Col. 0029D]; for in some Bibles they are placed in the body, and in others in the margin. Likewise, they debate whether the title of the Creed of Saint Athanasius truly belongs wholly or partly to that holy Father; whether the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* is rightly attributed to Ambrose and Augustine; and other similar questions. If, then, writings transcribed from the Fathers and doctors are brought back under examination after so many centuries have passed, why should we be surprised to find errors and inversions of clauses and prayers in the Gothic Office, transcribed partly during the period of Muslim rule and partly immediately after that rule had been overthrown?

Saint Isidore is not the sole author of the Gothic Breviary, nor was the liturgy that we see in the Isidorian Missal instituted at one time. The order for celebrating the canonical hours, too, was not polished all at once; rather, over the course of time, the Gothic Fathers and doctors partly retained the ancient Roman rite, partly excerpted material from Ambrose and other Italian doctors [Col. 0030A], and partly added material of their own. For when every bishop was granted authority to arrange divine worship, distinguished prelates of the Church were free to compose prayers and order petitions.

The Roman Church does not disdain to confess that it has borrowed a great deal from other Churches throughout the world. Gregory the Great himself replied to his detractors that he had borrowed certain elements not only from the Greek Church in the order of the Mass—such as the threefold Greek repetition “Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison,” and also “Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus,” corresponding to the Greek *Agios, Agios, Agios*—but also from the Churches of Milan, Spain, and Gaul. And when he wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English, he granted him the option of adopting the order of any Church, whether Gallican or Roman [Col. 0030B].

The Litanies, or Greater Rogations, were instituted by Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne. Almost all the hymns were composed by Blessed Ambrose, Hilary, Prudentius, and other private doctors. The Commemoration of All the Dead was introduced by Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, on 2 November. Yet the Roman Church rightly adopted all these things.

In the Creed sung in the Church, everyone readily admits that the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, expressed by the words “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son,” was solemnly proclaimed by the Fathers at the Third Council of Toledo. It is also highly probable that, when the Roman Church decreed that “Glory be to the Father, etc.” should be said at the end of each psalm, it followed the custom of the Spanish Fathers established at the Fourth Council of Toledo, namely, that the words of the Apocalypse, “Glory and honor, etc.,” should always be pronounced at the conclusion of the psalms [Col. 0030C]. And if Saint Damasus was Spanish, our assertion will have still greater force.

The Latins borrowed certain feasts from the Greeks, and the Greeks likewise from the Latins, without thereby confusing the Office of either Church or detracting anything from the antiquity of the Roman liturgy or from Saints Gregory the Great, John Chrysostom, or Isidore.

Finally, let us disclose unequivocal signs by which we demonstrate that our Gothic rite has in no way been altered. First, the Psalter has been printed in the same words in which it is found written in the very ancient Gothic Codex of Toledo [Col. 0030D]. Second, the seasonal prayers throughout the yearly cycle agree, apart from a few words, with the Veronese rite and the other Gothic rites, as will be evident to those who read Blanchini and Pinius. Third, the order of the prayers, and finally everything added in the Isidorian Breviary, agrees with the decrees of the Fourth Council of Toledo.

Let us examine again the passages of Saint Isidore concerning the divine Offices, and we shall see this Gothic rite of ours as clearly as midday. In Book I, chapter 5, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, speaking of the psalms, he asserts:

> The Psalter of sweet songs is frequently used by the Church, so that minds may more easily be bent toward compunction.

Here is the melody that is still retained to this day in our Church of Toledo as a remnant of the Gothic chant in certain verses and responsories [Col. 0031A], with a teacher of melodic chant assigned to instruct the boys, although this practice has already been obliterated in other Churches that have embraced Gregorian chant in every respect.

Let us pass to other testimonies of Saint Isidore. In chapter 10, concerning readings, after first recommending silence so that the readings may be understood by the hearers, he adds these words:

> Therefore the deacon also urges silence in a clear voice.

Here are the words that the deacon repeatedly says before the readings in the Mozarabic rite:

> Keep silence.

Unless I am mistaken, we do not read these words in the more recent Roman order.

In chapter 11, concerning the books of the Testaments, he takes it for granted that readings are pronounced and sung from both Testaments, the Old and the New. This is observed with exactness in the sacrifice of the Mass [Col. 0031B] according to the Gothic rite, for the first Epistle is taken from the Old Testament and the second from the New Testament.

Finally, to pass over other matters, in chapter 13, concerning praises—that is, the *alleluia*, or *lauda*, as the Mozarabic priests call it—the holy doctor says:

> In the regions of Africa, *ALLELUIA* is not sung at every time, but only on Sundays and during the fifty days after the Resurrection, as a sign of the future Resurrection and of joy. But among us, according to the ancient tradition of the Spains, it is sung at all times except on days of fasting or Lent; for it is written: “His praise shall always be in my mouth.”

Here is the foundation and reason why the Mozarabs sing the *alleluia* even in the Mass for the dead, something that had fallen out of use in the Roman Church so many centuries ago [Col. 0031C].

In the manuscripts of this Breviary of ours, observe that from Canticle LVIII up to but excluding the last one, after the book of Sacred Scripture from which each canticle is taken has been noted, the following notation is placed beside the first: “XVIII. *Praeceptum*”; beside the next: “XXXV. *In tuo*”; and in the margin there is this sign, which in our manuscripts signifies Matins. The purpose was to indicate to readers the canticles assigned to the Lauds, as well as the antiphons corresponding to the psalms. Observe that the words *praeceptum* and *in tuo* are the beginnings of the antiphons that precede the psalms; the same thing occurs with the canticles.

On the Saturday before the Third Sunday of Lent, at the hour of Terce, a reading is assigned from Proverbs, chapter XXIV [Col. 0031D]. In the verse “The righteous man falls seven times,” the words “in a day” are added, although they are found neither in the Vulgate nor in any other translation of the Bible.

On the Thursday before Pentecost, the first prayer at None appears very clearly to have been derived from Saint Augustine’s exposition of the words of Psalm LXXI, “Let the mountains receive peace, and the hills righteousness.” The holy doctor interprets these words in *Tractate I on the Gospel of Saint John*:

> The lofty souls are the mountains; the little souls are the hills. But the mountains receive peace for this reason: so that the hills may be able to receive righteousness. What is the righteousness that the hills receive? Faith . . . . But the lesser souls would not receive faith unless the greater souls, which are called mountains, were illumined by Wisdom herself, so that they might transmit to the little ones what the little ones are able to receive, and so that the hills might live by faith, because the mountains receive peace.
