## At Terce

**Ecclesiastes** (last chapter).

**R.** Thanks be to God.

My son, although Ecclesiastes was wise, he taught the people and recounted what he had done; and, investigating, he composed many proverbs, which are useful words. He wrote holy sayings, utterly upright and full of truth. The words of the wise are like goads and like nails driven deep, given through the counsel of masters by one shepherd. Beyond these things, my son, seek nothing further. Of making many books there is no end, and frequent meditation is an affliction of the flesh. For this is the whole of humanity: God brings everything that is done into judgment for every offense, whether it is good or evil. Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter. Fear God and observe his commandments.

[Col. 0408A]

**Reading from the Book of Joshua** (Chapter XXIV).

**R.** Thanks be to God.

In those days: Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel at Shechem and summoned the elders, princes, judges, and magistrates; and they stood in the sight of the Lord. He spoke to the people as follows:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Beyond the river your fathers dwelt from the beginning—Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor—and they served foreign gods. Therefore I took your father Abraham from the borders of Mesopotamia and brought him into the land of Canaan. I multiplied his offspring and gave him Isaac; and to him again I gave Mount Seir to possess. But Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt.

“I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with many signs and wonders. I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. The Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and cavalry as far as the Red Sea. Then the Israelites cried out to the Lord, who placed darkness between you and the Egyptians, and brought the sea over them and covered them. Our eyes saw all that he did in Egypt. You dwelt in the wilderness for a long time, and he brought you into the land of the Amorite who lived beyond the Jordan. When they fought against you, he delivered them into your hands; you took possession of their land and killed them.

“Then Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. He sent for Balaam son of Beor, to curse you; but I was unwilling to listen to him. On the contrary, through him I blessed you and rescued you from his hand.

“You crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho. The men of the city fought against you—the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—and I delivered them into your hands. I sent hornets before you, and I drove them out from their places: the two kings of the Amorites—not by your sword or your bow. I gave you a land for which you had not labored, and cities which you had not built, so that you might dwell in them; vineyards and olive groves which you had not planted.

“Now therefore fear the Lord and serve him with a perfect and most sincere heart. Remove the gods whom your fathers served in Mesopotamia and in Egypt, and serve the Lord. But if it seems evil to you not to serve him, you have a choice: choose today what pleases you, whom you ought above all to serve—whether the gods whom your fathers served in Mesopotamia, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we shall serve the Lord.”

The people answered and said: “Far be it from us to abandon the Lord and serve foreign gods. The Lord our God himself brought us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. He performed great signs before our eyes and guarded us on the whole way along which we walked, and among all the peoples through whom we passed. He drove out all the nations, the Amorite who inhabited the land into which we entered. Therefore we shall serve the Lord, for he is our God.”

Joshua said to the people: “You will not be able to serve the Lord, for he is holy, strong, and jealous; and he will not forgive your crimes and sins. If you abandon him for foreign gods, he will turn against you, afflict you, and overthrow you after he has bestowed gifts upon you.”

The people said: “Certainly not; rather, we shall serve the Lord.”

And Joshua said to the people: “You are witnesses that you yourselves have chosen the Lord, to serve him.”

They answered: “We are witnesses.”

“Now therefore,” he said, “remove the foreign gods from among you and incline your hearts toward the Lord God of Israel.”

The people said to Joshua: “We shall serve the Lord our God and obey his commandments.”

Thus Joshua made a covenant with the people on that day and set before them statutes and judgments at Shechem. He wrote all these words in the book of the law of God. Then he took a great stone and placed it beneath the oak that was in the sanctuary of the Lord. And he said to all the people:

“Behold, this stone shall be a witness for you, because it has heard all the words of the Lord that he spoke to you, lest afterward you should wish to deny them and lie to the Lord your God.”

Then he dismissed the people, each to his own possession.

After these things Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten. They buried him within the boundaries of his possession at Thamnath, situated on Mount Ephraim, on the northern side of Mount Gaash. Israel served the Lord throughout all the days of Joshua.

**R.** Amen.

**Reading from the Book of the Prophet Daniel** (Chapter III).

**R.** Thanks be to God.

Blessed are you, O Lord, God of our fathers, and praised and glorious is your name forever, because you are just in all that you have done for us; all your works are true, your ways are right, and all your judgments are true. For you have carried out true judgments in accordance with all that you have brought upon us and upon the holy city of our fathers, Jerusalem, because in truth and judgment you have brought all these things upon us because of our sins.

For we have sinned and acted wickedly by turning away from you; we have offended in everything and have not listened to your commandments, nor done as you commanded us, so that it might go well with us. Therefore all that you have brought upon us and everything that you have done to us, you have done in true judgment. You have handed us over to unjust and exceedingly wicked enemies, to a lawless and utterly evil king, more wicked than all the earth.

And now we cannot open our mouths; we have become a disgrace and a reproach to your servants and to those who worship you. Do not, we beg, hand us over forever because of your name, and do not destroy your covenant. Do not take your mercy from us because of Abraham, your beloved, Isaac, your servant, and Israel, your holy one, to whom you spoke, promising that you would multiply their offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand upon the seashore.

For, O Lord, we have been diminished more than all the nations, and today we are humbled throughout the whole earth because of our sins. At this time there is neither prince nor prophet nor leader, neither burnt offering nor sacrifice nor offering nor incense nor place for firstfruits before you, so that we might find mercy. But may we be received with a contrite soul and a humble spirit. As with the burnt offering of rams and bulls, and as with thousands of fat lambs, so may our sacrifice be in your sight today, so that it may please you; and bring to perfection those who follow you, because there is no shame for those who trust in you.

And now we follow you with all our heart, fear you, and seek your face. Do not put us to shame.

## At Lauds

**Antiphon.** Turn your face away from our sins, O God, and blot out all our iniquities.

Psalm L.

**Prayer.** Turn your face away from our sins, O Lord, and blot out all our iniquities. Remove from your eyes the crime of our evil pleasures, and mercifully incline your hearing to our confession. Have mercy, we beseech you, on us who ask, you who look favorably upon us in adversity and grant a repentant heart to those in despair; do not in any way turn away from our confessions.

Therefore, since you are appeased by the sacrifices of a contrite heart, grant us to offer you what you command and to deserve the forgiveness that your grace promises. But since the Publican, standing far away and beating his breast, was cleansed by confession alone, hear us sinners likewise, so that just as you granted him the fruit of his petition according to his merit, so you may deign to bestow forgiveness of sins upon us, your unworthy servants, who make supplication.

[Col. 0413B]

**Reading from the Book of Judges** (Chapter VI).

**R.** Thanks be to God.

In those days: The Israelites did evil in the sight of the Lord, who delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years, and they were greatly oppressed by them. They made for themselves caves and grottoes in the mountains, and very strongly fortified places in which to resist. Whenever Israel had sown, Midian, Amalek, and the other eastern peoples would come up, pitch their tents among them, and devastate everything as far as the entrance of Gaza. They left nothing at all in Israel that was necessary for life—neither sheep, nor oxen, nor donkeys.

For they and all their flocks came with their tents and filled everything like locusts: an innumerable multitude of people and camels, destroying whatever they touched. Israel was greatly humbled before Midian and cried out to the Lord, seeking help against the Midianites.

The Lord sent them a prophet and spoke: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I made you come up from Egypt, brought you out of the house of slavery, rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and of all the enemies who afflicted you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land. I said: ‘I am the Lord your God; do not fear the land of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.’ But you were unwilling to listen to my voice.”

Then an angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the oak that was in Ophrah and belonged to Joash, father of the family of Ezri. While Gideon his son was threshing and cleaning grain in the winepress to escape Midian, the angel appeared to him and said: “The Lord is with you, bravest of men.”

Gideon said to him: “I beg you, my lord, if the Lord is with us, why have all these things overtaken us? Where are his wonders, which our fathers recounted and said, ‘The Lord brought us up from Egypt’? But now he has abandoned us and delivered us into the hands of Midian.”

The Lord looked upon him and said: “Go in this strength of yours, and you will rescue Israel from the hand of Midian. Know that I have sent you.”

He answered: “I beg you, my lord, with what shall I rescue Israel? Behold, my family is weak in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.”

The Lord said to him: “I will be with you, and you will strike Midian as one man.”

And he said: “If I have found favor before you, give me a sign that you are the one speaking with me. Do not depart from here until I return to you, carrying a sacrifice and offering it to you.”

He answered: “I will await your return.”

So Gideon entered, cooked a kid, and made unleavened loaves from a measure of flour. He placed the meat in a basket, poured the broth into a pot, carried everything beneath the oak, and offered it to him. The angel of the Lord said to him: “Take the unleavened loaves and the meat, place them upon that rock, and pour the broth over them.”

When he had done so, the angel of the Lord stretched out the tip of the staff that he held in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened loaves. Fire rose from the rock and consumed them, and the angel of the Lord vanished from his sight.

When Gideon saw that he was the angel of the Lord, he said: “Alas, Lord God, for I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face!”

The Lord said to him: “Peace be with you; do not fear; you will not die.”

So Gideon built an altar there to the Lord and called it “The Lord Is Peace,” to the present day.

**R.** Amen.

## At Terce

[Col. 0414C]

**The Wisdom of Solomon** (Chapter XVII).

**V.** Thanks be to God.

My son, great are the judgments of the Lord and ineffable are his works; therefore undisciplined souls have gone astray. For while the wicked suppose that they can rule a holy nation, bound by fetters of darkness and shackles of the long night, shut up beneath roofs, fugitives from eternal providence, they lie there. And while they think they are hidden in obscure sins, they are scattered beneath the dark veil of forgetfulness, trembling horribly and greatly disturbed with immense astonishment.

For the cave that held them did not guard them without fear, since a descending sound disturbed them, and grim faces appearing caused them terror. Fire could provide them with no light, nor could the clear flames of the stars illuminate that dreadful night. But a sudden fire appeared to them, full of fear; and, struck with terror at the face that could not be seen, they judged the things that were visible to be worse. They were subjected to the mockery of magical art, and the rebuke of their vaunted wisdom came with insult.

A heavy night had been imposed upon them alone, an image of the darkness that was destined to come upon them. Thus they themselves were heavier than darkness to themselves, but for your holy ones there was great light.

**R.** Amen.

**Reading from the Book of Judges** (Chapter VI).

**R.** Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0415A]

In those days: All Midian, Amalek, and the eastern peoples gathered together, crossed the Jordan, and encamped in the valley of Jezreel. The Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon; and he sounded the trumpet and summoned the house of Abiezer to follow him. He sent messengers throughout Manasseh, which also followed him, and other messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, who came out to meet him.

Gideon said to the Lord: “If you save Israel by my hand, as you have said, I will place this fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone and dryness over all the ground, I shall know that by my hand, as you have said, you will save Israel.”

And it happened so. Rising at night, he wrung out the fleece and filled a bowl with dew. He said again to the Lord: “Let not your anger burn against me if I test once more, seeking a sign in the fleece. I ask that the fleece alone be dry and that all the ground be wet with dew.”

And God did so that night as he had asked: dryness was upon the fleece alone, and dew upon all the ground.

**(Chapter VII.)** Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, rising at night, and all the people with him, came to the spring called Harod. The camp of Midian was in the valley, north of the high hill.

The Lord said to Gideon: “The people with you are too numerous, and Midian will not be delivered into their hands, lest Israel boast against me and say, ‘I was saved by my own strength.’ Speak to the people and proclaim in the hearing of all: ‘Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return.’”

So twenty thousand men withdrew from Mount Gilead and returned from the people, and only ten thousand remained.

The Lord said to Gideon: “There are still too many people. Lead them to the waters, and there I will test them. Those of whom I say to you, ‘Let them go with you,’ shall go; whoever I reject shall return.”

When the people had gone down to the waters, the Lord said to Gideon: “Separate those who lap the water with their tongues, as dogs are accustomed to lap, by themselves; but those who drink on bended knees shall be on the other side.”

The number of those who lapped the water, bringing it to their mouths with their hands, was three hundred men; the entire remaining multitude had drunk kneeling. The Lord said to Gideon: “By the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver Midian into your hand; let all the remaining multitude return to its place.”

So he took provisions and trumpets in proportion to their number, ordered the entire remaining multitude to go to their tents, and committed himself to battle with the three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below in the valley.

That same night the Lord said to him: “Rise and go down into the camp, for I have delivered them into your hand. But if you fear going alone, let Phurah your servant go down with you. When you hear what they say, your hands will be strengthened, and you will go down more confidently against the enemy camp.”

So he went down, with Phurah his servant, to the part of the camp where the guards of the armed men were. Midian, Amalek, and all the eastern peoples lay spread out in the valley like a dense swarm of locusts; and their camels were innumerable, like the sand that lies on the seashore.

When Gideon had arrived, someone was recounting a dream to his companion and reporting what he had seen in this manner: “I saw a dream, and it seemed to me that a barley loaf baked under the ashes rolled down into the camp of Midian. When it reached a tent, it struck it, overturned it, and leveled it completely with the ground.”

The one to whom he spoke answered: “This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, an Israelite man. God has delivered Midian and its entire camp into his hands.”

When Gideon heard the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. He returned to the camp of Israel and said: “Rise, for the Lord has delivered the camp of Midian into our hands.”

He divided the three hundred men into three groups and gave trumpets into their hands, with empty jars and torches inside the jars. He said to them: “Do exactly what you see me do. I shall enter the part of the camp; follow what I do. When the trumpet sounds in my hand, you also sound the trumpets around the entire camp and cry out, ‘For the Lord and for Gideon!’”

Gideon and the three hundred men who were with him entered the part of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch of the night. When the guards had been roused, they began to sound the trumpets and smash the jars among themselves. When they had sounded the trumpets at three places around the camp and had broken the jars, they held the torches in their left hands and the sounding trumpets in their right, and cried: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon!” Each man stood in his place around the hostile camp.

The whole camp was thrown into confusion; they cried out and fled, while the three hundred men continued sounding the trumpets. The Lord set the sword of each against all the others throughout the camp, and they slaughtered one another. The fugitives fled as far as Bethseca, and to the border of Abelmehula at Tebbath.

The men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh shouted and pursued Midian. He sent messengers throughout the mountain country of Ephraim, saying: “Go down to meet Midian and seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.”

All Ephraim shouted and seized the waters and the Jordan as far as Beth-barah. They captured two men of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb. They pursued Midian, carrying the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon beyond the streams of the Jordan.

**R.** Amen.

**Antiphon 1.** May your mercy, O Lord, quickly come before us.

Psalm LXXVIII.

**Prayer.** May your mercy quickly anticipate us, O Lord—we whom neither the consolation of hope, nor confidence in merit, nor the assistance of help sustains, but whom, tossed amid guilt and afflictions, either the consciousness of crimes or the punishment of sins presses hard. Deliver us for the glory of your name, and be favorable to our sins for the sake of your name, so that when you have done both things for your sake and have looked upon your people with your customary goodness, glory may be given to you for our deliverance, and reconciliation may come to us through your name.

**R.** Amen.

Through mercy.

[Col. 0417A]

**Antiphon 2.** Rejoice in God our helper; shout for joy to the God of Jacob.

Psalm LXXX.

### At None

#### From the Wisdom of Solomon (Chapter 6)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

“My son, wisdom is better than strength, and a prudent man better than a strong man. Hear, therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who hold the multitude and take pride in crowds of nations, because power has been given to you by the Lord and strength by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts.

“For although you were ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly, nor did you keep the law of justice, nor walk according to the will of God. He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because the severest judgment will be upon those who rule. For the lowly are granted mercy, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments. God, who is Lord of all, will not exempt anyone’s person from judgment, nor will he respect anyone’s greatness, because he himself made the small and the great, and he cares equally for all.”

**R.** Amen.

#### Reading from the Book of Judges (Chapter 8)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

“In those days, when Gideon had come to the Jordan, he crossed it with the three hundred men who were with him; yet because of exhaustion they could not pursue the fugitives. He said to the men of Succoth: ‘Give, I beg you, loaves to the people who are with me, for they are very weary, so that we may pursue Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian.’

“The princes of Succoth answered: ‘Perhaps the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna are already in your hand, and for this reason you ask us to give bread to your army?’ He said to them: ‘When the Lord has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hands, I will crush your flesh with the thorns and briars of the desert.’

“From there he went up to Penuel and spoke similar words to the men of that place. They too answered him as the men of Succoth had answered. So he said to them: ‘When I return victorious in peace, I will destroy this tower.’

“Now Zebah and Zalmunna were resting with their entire army. For fifteen thousand men remained from all the troops of the eastern peoples, while one hundred and twenty thousand warriors who drew the sword had been slain. Gideon went up by the road of those who dwelt in tents, east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and struck the camp of the enemy, who were secure and suspected nothing adverse.

“Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but Gideon pursued and captured them, while their entire army was thrown into confusion. Returning from battle before sunrise, he seized a young man from the men of Succoth and questioned him about the names of the princes and elders of Succoth; and he wrote down seventy-seven men. He came to Succoth and said to them: ‘Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, concerning whom you reproached me, saying: “Perhaps the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna are in your hands, and for this reason you ask us to give bread to men who are weary and exhausted.”’

“Then he took the elders of the city, along with the thorns and briars of the desert, and with them crushed and mangled the men of Succoth. He also overturned the tower of Penuel and killed the inhabitants of the city.

“He said to Zebah and Zalmunna: ‘What sort of men were those whom you killed at Tabor?’ They answered: ‘They were like you, and one of them was like the son of a king.’ He said: ‘They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the Lord lives, if you had spared them, I would not kill you.’

“He said to Jether, his firstborn: ‘Rise and kill them.’ But he did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a boy. Zebah and Zalmunna said: ‘Rise yourself and fall upon us, for a man’s strength corresponds to his age.’

“Gideon rose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the ornaments and pendants with which the necks of royal camels are customarily adorned. All the men of Israel said to Gideon: ‘Rule over us—you, your son, and your son’s son—for you have delivered us from the hand of Midian.’

“He answered them: ‘I will not rule over you, nor will my son rule over you; the Lord will rule over you.’

“And he said to them: ‘I ask one request of you: give me the earrings from your spoil.’ For the Ishmaelites were accustomed to have gold earrings. They answered: ‘We will gladly give them.’ They spread out a cloak upon the ground and threw the earrings from the spoil into it. The weight of the earrings he had requested was one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold, apart from the ornaments, pendants, and purple garments that the kings of Midian were accustomed to wear, and apart from the golden necklaces of the camels.

“Gideon made an ephod from these things and placed it in his city, Ephra. All Israel fornicated with it, and it became a ruin to Gideon and to his whole house.

“Midian was humbled before the children of Israel and could no longer lift up its head; and the land rested for forty years, during which Gideon ruled.

“Jerubbaal, son of Joash, went away and lived in his own house. He had seventy sons who came forth from his thigh, because he had many wives. His concubine, whom he had in Shechem, bore him a son named Abimelech.

“Gideon, son of Joash, died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father.”

**R.** Amen.

#### Reading from the Book of Judges (Chapter 13)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

“In those days there was a certain man from Zorah, from the tribe of Dan, named Manoah, who had a barren wife. The Angel of the Lord appeared to her and said: ‘You are barren and without children, but you will conceive and bear a son, whose head no razor shall touch. For he will be a Nazirite from his infancy, and from his mother’s womb he will begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.’

“When she came to her husband, she said to him: ‘A man of God came to me, with an angelic countenance, exceedingly terrifying. When I asked him who he was, or where he had come from, or by what name he was called, he would not tell me. But he answered this: “Behold, you will conceive and bear a son. Beware that you drink no wine or strong drink and eat nothing unclean. For the boy will be a Nazirite from his infancy, and from his mother’s womb until the day of his death.”’

“Manoah prayed to the Lord and said: ‘I beg you, Lord, let the man whom you sent come again and teach us what we ought to do concerning the boy who is to be born.’

“The Lord heard Manoah’s prayer, and the Angel of the Lord appeared again to his wife as she was sitting in the field. Manoah her husband was not with her. When she saw the Angel, she hurried and ran to her husband. She said to him: ‘Behold, he has appeared to me, whom I saw before.’

“He rose and followed his wife. Coming to the man, he said to him: ‘Are you the one who spoke to the woman?’ He answered: ‘I am.’

“Manoah said to him: ‘When your word has been fulfilled, what do you wish the boy to do? What must we observe?’

“The Angel of the Lord said to Manoah: ‘Let him abstain from everything that I said to your wife. Let him eat nothing that comes from the vine; let him drink no wine or strong drink; let him eat nothing unclean; and let him fulfill and observe what I commanded him.’

“Manoah said to the Angel of the Lord: ‘I beg you to consent to my prayers, and we will prepare for you a kid from the goats.’

“The Angel of the Lord answered him: ‘If you compel me, I will not eat your bread; but if you wish to offer a burnt offering, offer it to God.’ Manoah did not know that he was the Angel of the Lord.

“He said to him: ‘What is your name, so that when your word has been fulfilled we may honor you?’

“He answered him: ‘My name is Wonderful.’

“Manoah therefore took a kid from the goats and libations, and placed them upon a rock, offering them to the Lord, who works wonders. He and his wife were watching. As the flame of the altar rose toward heaven, the Angel of the Lord ascended in the flame as well.

“When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell on their faces to the ground, and the Angel of the Lord no longer appeared to them. Immediately Manoah understood that he was the Angel of the Lord and said to his wife: ‘We shall surely die, because we have seen God.’

“The woman answered him: ‘If the Lord wished to kill us, he would not have received a burnt offering and libations from our hands, nor shown us all these things, nor told us things that are to come.’

“She gave birth to a son and called his name Samson. The boy grew, and the Lord blessed him. The Spirit of the Lord began to be with him.”

**R.** Amen.

## At Terce

#### From Ecclesiasticus of Solomon (Chapter 25)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

“My son, every wound is sorrow of heart, and every wickedness is the wickedness of a woman. Every wound—and not the wound of the heart—he will see; every wickedness—and not the wickedness of a woman; every covering—and not the covering of those who hate; every vengeance—and not the vengeance of enemies.

“There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and there is no anger above the anger of an enemy. It would be more pleasing to dwell with a lion or a dragon than to live with a wicked woman.

“A woman’s wickedness changes her face; she darkens her countenance like a bear and displays herself as though she were a sack. In the midst of their neighbors her husband groans, and hearing her he sighs softly.

“Every wickedness is brief compared with the wickedness of a woman; may the lot of sinners fall upon her. As a sandy ascent is to the feet of an old man, so is a talkative woman to a quiet man.

“If a woman has the first place, she is contrary to her husband. A humble heart, a sorrowful face, and a wound unto death are found in a wicked woman. Weak hands and trembling knees belong to a woman who does not make her husband happy.

“From a woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die. A strong woman delights her husband and fills his years with life in peace.”

**R.** Amen.

#### Reading from the Book of Judges (Chapter 14)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

“In those days Samson went down to Timnah. Seeing there a woman from the daughters of the Philistines, he went up and announced it to his father and mother, saying: ‘I have seen a woman in Timnah, from the daughters of the Philistines. I ask you to take her for me as a wife.’

“His father and mother said to him: ‘Is there no woman among the daughters of your brothers, or among all my people, that you wish to take a wife from the Philistines, who are uncircumcised?’

“Samson said to his father: ‘Take this one for me, because she has pleased my eyes.’

“His parents did not know that the matter was from the Lord, who was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines, who ruled over Israel.

“Samson therefore went down with his father and mother to Timnah. When they came to the vineyards of the town, a fierce young lion appeared, roaring, and ran to meet him. The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, and he tore the lion apart as one might tear a kid into pieces, having absolutely nothing in his hand. But he did not tell his father this.

“He went down and spoke to the woman who had pleased his eyes. After some days, when he returned to take her, he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion. And behold, a swarm of bees was in the lion’s mouth, and there was a honeycomb. Taking it in his hands, he ate it as he went; and coming to his father and mother, he gave them some, and they too ate. Yet he did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the body of the lion.

“His father went down to the woman, and Samson made a feast there. For this was the custom of young men. When the citizens of the place saw him, they gave him companions to be with him—thirty men.

“Samson said to them: ‘I will propose a riddle to you. If you solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and as many tunics. But if you cannot solve it, you will give me thirty linen garments and the same number of tunics.’

“They answered him: ‘Propose the riddle, so that we may hear it.’

“He said to them: ‘Out of the eater came food, and out of the strong came sweetness.’

“For three days they could not solve the riddle. When the seventh day arrived, they said to Samson’s wife: ‘Entice your husband and persuade him to tell you what the riddle means. If you will not do this, we will burn you and your father’s house. Did you invite us to the wedding for this purpose—to strip us?’

“She wept before Samson and complained, saying: ‘You hate me and do not love me. For this reason you will not explain to me the riddle that you proposed to the sons of my people.’

“He answered her: ‘I did not wish to tell it to my father and mother, and should I tell it to you?’

“For seven days of the feast she wept before him. At last, on the seventh day, when she pressed him, he explained it to her. She immediately told it to her fellow citizens. They said to him on the seventh day before sunset: ‘What is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?’

“He said to them: ‘If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have discovered my riddle.’

“Then the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him. He went down to Ashkelon and struck thirty men. He took their garments and gave them to those who had solved the riddle. Being exceedingly angry, he went up to his father’s house. His wife was given to his companion and wedding attendant.

### Chapter 15

“After some time, when the days of the wheat harvest were approaching, Samson came, wishing to visit his wife, and brought her a kid from the goats. When he intended, as usual, to enter her bedroom, her father prevented him, saying: ‘I thought you hated her, and therefore I gave her to your companion. But she has a sister who is younger and more beautiful than she is; let her be your wife instead.’

“Samson answered him: ‘From this day there will be no blame on me against the Philistines; for I will do evil to you.’

“He went away and caught three hundred foxes. He joined their tails together and tied torches in the middle. After setting them on fire, he released them to run here and there. They immediately went into the fields of the Philistines. When these had been set alight, the grain that had already been gathered, as well as the standing crops, was burned, so thoroughly that the flame also consumed the vineyards and olive groves.

“The Philistines said: ‘Who has done this thing?’

“They were told: ‘Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to another; this is what he has done.’

“The Philistines went up and burned both the woman and her father.

“Samson said to them: ‘Although you have done this, I will nevertheless exact vengeance from you, and only then will I rest.’

“He struck them with a great slaughter, so that they were stunned and placed thigh upon thigh. He went down and lived in the cave of the rock of Etam.

“Then the Philistines went up into the land of Judah and encamped in the place that was afterward called Lechi—that is, Jawbone—where their army was scattered. The men of the tribe of Judah said to them: ‘Why have you come up against us?’

“They answered: ‘We have come to bind Samson and repay him for what he has done to us.’

“Three thousand men of Judah went down to the cave of the rock of Etam and said to Samson: ‘Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why did you wish to do this?’

“He said to them: ‘As they did to me, so I have done to them.’

“They said: ‘We have come to bind you and hand you over to the Philistines.’

“He said: ‘Swear to me that you will not kill me.’

“They answered: ‘We will not kill you.’

“They bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock of Etam. When he came to the place of Jawbone and the Philistines came shouting to meet him, the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him. As wood is customarily consumed by the heat of fire, so the cords with which he had been bound were broken apart and loosened.

“Finding a jawbone—that is, the jawbone of a donkey—which lay there, he seized it and killed a thousand men with it. He said: ‘With the jawbone of a donkey, with the jawbone of a young donkey, I have wiped them out; I have struck a thousand men.’

“When he had completed these words in song, he threw the jawbone from his hand and called the name of that place Ramath-lechi, which means ‘lifting up of the jawbone.’

“Being very thirsty, he cried out to the Lord and said: ‘You have given this great salvation and victory into the hand of your servant, and behold, I am dying of thirst and shall fall into the hands of the uncircumcised.’

“Then the Lord opened the molar tooth in the jawbone of the donkey, and water came out of it. When he had drunk, his spirit was refreshed and he recovered his strength. Therefore the name of that place was called ‘the Spring of the One Who Calls from the Jawbone,’ even to the present day.”

#### Reading from the Book of the Prophet Hosea (Chapter 4)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

“Hear the word of the Lord, sons of Israel, for the Lord has a dispute with the inhabitants of the land. There is no truth, no mercy, and no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing, lying, murder, theft, and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood.

“Because of this the land will mourn, and everyone who dwells in it will languish, together with the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky; even the fish of the sea will be gathered up.

“Yet no one should judge, nor should anyone be reproved, for your people are like those who contradict the priest. You will fall today, and the prophet will fall with you. At night I have silenced your mother.

“My people have been silent because they have lacked knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve as my priest. And because you have forgotten the law of your God, I too will forget your children.

“According to their multitude, so they sinned against me; I will change their glory into disgrace. They will eat the sins of my people and lift up their souls toward their iniquity. And it will be: as the people, so the priest. I will visit his ways upon him and repay him according to his thoughts.

“They will eat and not be satisfied; they have fornicated and have not ceased, because they abandoned the Lord by failing to keep his commandments. Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart.

“My people have asked counsel of their piece of wood, and their staff has announced it to them, for the spirit of fornication has deceived them, and they have fornicated against their God.

“They sacrificed upon the tops of the mountains and burned incense upon the hills, beneath oak, poplar, and terebinth, because its shade was good. Therefore your daughters will fornicate, and your brides will commit adultery.

“I will not visit your daughters when they have fornicated, nor your brides when they have committed adultery, because the men themselves consorted with prostitutes and sacrificed with effeminate men; and the people without understanding will be beaten.

“If you fornicate, Israel, let Judah at least not transgress. Do not enter Gilgal, nor go up to Beth-aven, and do not swear: ‘As the Lord lives.’

“For Israel has turned aside like a wanton cow; now the Lord will feed them like a lamb in a desert.”

#### Antiphon 1

I lifted my face to the Lord God, that I might find prayer and mercy. In fasting I prayed to the Lord God and said: You are the great and merciful Lord God, who keeps the covenant with those who love your law.

**V.** Lord God of hosts, who is like you? You are powerful, O Lord, and your truth is all around you. Psalm 88.

245 **Prayer.** Admirable Christ Jesus, Son of God, before whom none among the sons of God is found either equal or similar, to you, Lord, we direct our prayer. May you deign to extend to those who have been converted the mercy that you promised to preserve for the holy.

And so, we beseech you, correct us by the discipline of your governance, so that you do not remove clemency in anger. Let your covenant not be profaned because of the crimes committed; rather, let vengeance be tempered by heavenly mercy. May you yourself wash away everything that is displeasing—the one who glorifies sinners returning to you by justifying them—and you who willed that we should be what we are from nothing: grant that, made fit for the heavenly kingdoms, we may live with you without end.

**R.** Amen.

Through your mercy, our God, etc.

Through your mercy.

**P.** Now have mercy.

May the allurements of the age not hold them forever captive, so that the light of your face may make those already blessed shine.

Our Father.

“Hear this, princes of Jacob and rulers of the house of Israel: Is it not yours to know judgment, you who hate good and love evil, who violently strip their skin from them and their flesh from their bones?

“Yet I am filled with the strength of the spirit of the Lord, with judgment and truth.”

Therefore deliver us, O Lord, from the hand of hateful spirits and redeem us from the snares of our enemies. May we who believe your word be fortified by the strength of that very faith, 246 and thus may the confession of the humble ascend to the heights of heaven, so that salvation poured forth from your Word may come to our aid.

**Reading from the Book of Judges (Chapter XIX)**

**R.** Thanks be to God.

In those days, there was a certain Levite living on the flank of Mount Ephraim, who took a wife from Bethlehem of Judah. She left him and returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem, and remained there for four months. Her husband followed her, wishing to be reconciled with her, to speak kindly to her, and to bring her back with him; he had with him a servant and two donkeys. She received him and brought him into her father’s house.

When her father-in-law heard this and saw him, he went to meet him joyfully and embraced the man. The son-in-law remained in his father-in-law’s house for three days, eating and drinking familiarly with him. On the fourth day, rising during the night, he wished to depart. His father-in-law detained him and said: “First taste a little bread and strengthen your stomach, and then you may depart.” They sat together and ate and drank.

The girl’s father said to his son-in-law: “I ask you to remain here today, and let us rejoice together.” But he rose and began to wish to depart. Nevertheless, his father-in-law earnestly detained him and made him remain with him.

When morning came, the Levite was preparing for the journey. His father-in-law said to him again: “I beg you to take a little food and, having gained strength, wait until the day grows, and afterward depart.” So they ate together.

The young man rose to continue with his wife and servant. His father-in-law spoke to him again: “Consider that the day has declined toward sunset and is drawing toward evening. Remain with me today also, spend a joyful day, and tomorrow you may depart to go to your home.”

The son-in-law did not wish to comply with his words, but rose at once and came opposite Jebus, which is otherwise called Jerusalem, taking with him two laden donkeys and his concubine. They were already near Jebus, and the day was changing into night. The servant said to his master: “Come, I beg you, let us turn aside into the city of the Jebusites and spend the night there.”

His master answered him: “I will not enter a city of a foreign people who are not among the children of Israel, but I will pass on as far as Gibeah. When I arrive there, let us remain there—or, at least, in the city of Ramah.”

Thus they passed by Jebus and continued on their way. The sun set for them near Gibeah, which is in the tribe of Benjamin, and they turned aside to it to remain there. When they had entered, they sat in the city square, and no one wished to receive them as guests.

And behold, an old man appeared, returning in the evening from his field and his work. He too was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living as a resident alien in [Col. 0431A] Gibeah. The men of that region were descendants of Jemini.

The old man lifted his eyes and saw a man sitting in the city square with his bundles. He said to him: “Where do you come from, and where are you going?”

He answered him: “We have set out from Bethlehem of Judah and are going to our own place, which is on the flank of Mount Ephraim; from there we had gone to Bethlehem, and now we are going to the house of God. No one wishes to receive us under his roof. We have straw and hay for fodder for the donkeys, and bread and wine for my needs, for those of your maidservant, and for the servant who is with me. We lack nothing except lodging.”

The old man answered: “Peace be with you. I shall provide everything that is necessary; only, I beg you, do not remain in the square.”

He brought him into his house and provided fodder for the donkeys. After they had washed their feet, he received them at table.

While they were feasting and, after the labor of the journey, restoring their bodies with food and drink, men of that city, sons of Belial—that is, “without a yoke”—came and surrounded the old man’s house. They began to knock at the doors, shouting to the master of the house and saying: “Bring out the man who entered your house, so that we may abuse him.”

The old man went out to them and said: “No, my brothers, do not commit this evil. He has entered my house as a guest; stop this folly. I have a virgin daughter, and this man has a concubine. I shall bring them out to you, so that you may humiliate them and satisfy your lust. Only, I beg you, do not perpetrate this unnatural crime against the man.”

They would not listen to his words. Seeing this, the man brought out his concubine to them and handed her over to be mocked and abused. After they had used her throughout the whole night, they sent her away in the morning.

The woman, as the darkness was receding, came to the door of the house where her master was staying and collapsed there. When morning came, the man rose and opened the door in order to continue the journey he had begun. And behold, his concubine was lying before the door, with her hands spread across the threshold.

Thinking that she was resting, he spoke to her: “Rise, and let us go.” When she gave no answer, he understood that she was dead. He took her, placed her on the donkey, and returned to his house.

When he had entered, he seized a sword and cut the corpse of his wife, bones and all, into twelve parts and pieces, and sent them throughout all the borders of Israel.

When each person saw this, they cried out: “Never has such a thing happened in Israel, from the day our fathers came up from Egypt to the present time. Give your judgment and decide together what must be done.”

**(Chapter XX.)** Therefore all the children of Israel went out and gathered together as one man, from Dan to Beersheba, and the land of Gilead, before the Lord at Mizpah. All the corners of the peoples and all the tribes of Israel came together in the assembly of the people of God—forty thousand armed foot soldiers. (Nor was it hidden from the children of Benjamin that the children of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.)

The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, was asked how such a great crime had been committed, and he answered: “I came to Gibeah of Benjamin with my wife, and turned aside there. And behold, the men of that city surrounded the house in which I was staying during the night, wishing to kill me, and tormenting my wife with an incredible frenzy of lust; finally, she died.

“I seized her, cut her into pieces, and sent the parts throughout all the borders of your possession, because never has such a crime or such a great sacrilege been committed in Israel. You are all here, children of Israel; decide what you must do.”

All the people stood and answered as with one man’s voice: “We shall not return to our tents, nor shall anyone enter his own house. Instead, we shall act together against Gibeah. Let ten men be chosen from every hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, one hundred from every thousand, and one thousand from every ten thousand, to bring provisions for the army, so that we may fight against Gibeah of Benjamin and repay it for the crime it deserves.”

All Israel came together against the city as one man, with one mind and one purpose. They sent messengers to the whole tribe of Benjamin to say: “Why has such a great crime been found among you? Hand over the men of Gibeah who committed this outrage, so that they may die and the evil may be removed from Israel.”

But they would not listen to the command of their brothers, the children of Israel. Instead, they gathered at Gibeah from all the cities belonging to their lot, to bring them aid and fight against the whole people of Israel.

There were found twenty-five thousand men of Benjamin who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who numbered seven hundred very brave men, so left-handed that they fought as if with the right; they could sling stones with such accuracy that they could strike even a hair, and the stone’s blow would not deviate to either side.

Among the men of Israel, excluding the children of Benjamin, there were found forty thousand who drew the sword and were prepared for battle.

They rose and went up to the house of God—that is, to Shiloh—and consulted the Lord, saying: “Who shall be the leader of our army in the battle against the children of Benjamin?”

The Lord answered them: “Let Judah be your leader.”

At once the children of Israel rose in the morning and encamped near Gibeah. From there they advanced to battle against Benjamin and began to assault the city.

The children of Benjamin came out from Gibeah and killed twenty-two thousand men of Israel that day. Again the children of Israel, trusting in both their strength and their numbers, drew up their battle line in the same place where they had fought before. Yet first they went up and wept before the Lord until nightfall. They consulted God and said: “Should I continue to go out to fight against the children of Benjamin, my brothers, or not?”

He answered them: “Go up against them and engage in battle.”

When the children of Israel went out to battle against Benjamin on the following day, from the gates of Gibeah they encountered them, and they raged against them with such slaughter that they felled eighteen thousand men who drew the sword.

Therefore all the children of Israel came to the house of God, sat down, and wept before the Lord. They fasted that day until evening and offered him burnt offerings and peace offerings.  
**R.** Amen.

[Col. 0433A] **Hymn.** God, creator of all. fol. 175.

**Capitula.** We sing to you, O Christ, Redeemer and Lord and Judge, the festival of mercy and judgment: in the one you receive us, by the other you terrify us. There is the light of compassion; here the measure of examination. Grant, therefore, O Lord, to your suppliants that an evil heart may not cling to us, and that an evil thing may not present enticement before our eyes. Rather, as we walk in the simplicity of innocence, may you, merciful and gracious, extend yourself toward us and, as the true Judge, absolve us.

**Our Father.**

**Lauda.** Your hands made me and fashioned me.  
**P.** Give me understanding, O Lord, that I may learn your commandments.  
**V.** Those who fear you will see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word.  
**P.** Give me.  
**V.** Glory.  
**P.** Give me.

[Col. 0433B] **Prayer.** To you, O Lord, we lift our eyes, because we are the work of your hands. Give us understanding to learn your commandments, and fill those who fear you with joy. Let your mercy come to console us; may it both rescue us from every evil and teach us the dignity of works pleasing to you.  
**R.** Amen.

Through your mercy.

## At Terce

**Reading from the Book of Proverbs of Solomon (Chapter XXIV)**

**R.** Thanks be to God.

My son, Wisdom built herself a house, and prudence will strengthen it. The storerooms will be filled with learning, with every precious and beautiful substance. A wise man is strong, and a learned man robust and powerful. For war is undertaken with planning, and there is safety where there are many counsels.

Whoever thinks of doing evil will be called a fool. The thought of a fool is sin, and the slanderer is an abomination to men. If you lose hope when you are weary on the day of distress, your strength will diminish.

Rescue those who are being led to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction. If you say, “Our strength is insufficient,” he who examines the heart understands; nothing escapes the one who preserves your soul, and he will repay a person according to his works.

Do not lie in wait or seek wickedness in the house of the righteous, nor destroy his rest. For the righteous falls seven times a day and rises again, but the wicked will collapse into evil.

When your enemy falls, do not rejoice; when he is ruined, let your heart not exult, lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn his anger away from him.

Do not contend with the worst of men, nor envy the wicked, for the evil have no hope of what is to come, and the lamp of the wicked will be extinguished. Their destruction will suddenly arise, and who knows the ruin of either of them?

Do not be a needless witness against your neighbor, nor deceive anyone with your lips. Do not say: “As he did to me, so I shall do to him, and I shall repay each person according to his work.”  
**R.** Amen.

**Reading from the Book of Judges (Chapter XX)**

**R.** Thanks be to God.

In those days, the children of Israel consulted the Lord and said: “Should we go out again to fight against the children of Benjamin, our brothers, or should we rest?”

The Lord said to them: “Go up, for tomorrow I shall hand them over to you.”

The children of Israel placed ambushes around the city of Gibeah. For the third time, as once and twice before, they led out the army against Benjamin.

The children of Benjamin also boldly burst out of the city and pursued the fleeing enemy farther, so that they wounded some of them as on the first and second days and struck down their rear as they turned their backs along two roads, one of which led toward Bethel and the other toward Gibeah. They felled about thirty men, for they thought they were striking them as usual.

But the Israelites, feigning flight by strategy, planned to draw them away from the city and lead them, as though fleeing, toward the roads mentioned above. Then all the children of Israel rose from their positions and drew up their line at the place called Baal-tamar.

The ambushes that were around the city also gradually began to reveal themselves and advanced toward the western side of the city. Another ten thousand men from all Israel were challenging the inhabitants of the city to battle.

The battle grew fierce against the children of Benjamin, and they did not understand that destruction stood against them on every side. The Lord struck them down before the children of Israel, and they killed twenty-five thousand and one hundred of them that day, all warriors and men who drew the sword.

When the children of Benjamin saw that they were inferior, they began to flee. Seeing this, the children of Israel gave them room to flee, so that they might reach the ambushes they had placed near the city.

When the men in hiding suddenly rose and Benjamin turned its back, they entered the city and struck it with the edge of the sword. The children of Israel had given a signal to those whom they had placed in ambush: after they had captured the city, they were to set it on fire, so that the smoke rising high would show that the city had been captured.

When the children of Israel, engaged in the battle itself, saw this—for the children of Benjamin had thought that they were fleeing and had pursued them more vigorously, after thirty men of Israel's army had been killed—the Israelites looked back and saw that the city had been captured and that flames were rising upward. Those who had earlier feigned flight turned their faces and resisted valiantly.

When the children of Benjamin saw this, they fled and began to go toward the road of the wilderness, while their enemies pursued them there as well. The men who had set fire to the city also met them.

Thus it happened that they were struck down by enemies on both sides, and there was no respite for those who were dying. They fell and were slaughtered on the eastern side of the city of Gibeah.

Those killed there numbered eighteen thousand men, all very strong warriors. When those who remained of Benjamin saw this, they fled into the wilderness and continued toward the rock called Rimmon. In that flight, scattered and making for different places, they killed five thousand men. As they continued on, their pursuers overtook them and killed another two thousand.

Thus all the children of Benjamin who had fallen in various places numbered twenty-five thousand, warriors most ready for battle. Of the entire number of Benjamin, only six hundred men remained who had been able to escape and flee into the wilderness. They sat at the rock of Rimmon for four months.

The children of Israel returned and struck with the sword all the remaining inhabitants of the city, from men to animals, and voracious flame consumed all the cities and villages of Benjamin.

**(Chapter XXI.)** The children of Israel swore an oath at Mizpah, saying: “None of us shall give his daughter as a wife to the children of Benjamin.”

All came to the house of God at Shiloh and, sitting before him until evening, raised their voices and began to weep with great wailing, saying: “Why, O Lord God of Israel, has this evil happened among your people, so that today one tribe has been taken away from us?”

On the following day, rising at dawn, they built an altar. There they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and they said: “Who among all the tribes of Israel did not go up in the army of the Lord?” For they had bound themselves by a great oath at Mizpah to kill those who had been absent.

The children of Israel were moved to repentance over their brother Benjamin and began to say: “One tribe has been removed from Israel. From where will they obtain wives? For we all swore together that we would not give them our daughters.”

Therefore they said: “Who among all the tribes of Israel did not go up to the Lord at Mizpah?” And behold, the men of Jabesh-gilead were found not to have been in that army. (At that same time, when they were at Shiloh, none of them was found there either.)

So they sent ten thousand of the strongest men and commanded them: “Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword, both their wives and their little ones. This is what you must observe: kill every male and every woman who has known a man, but reserve the virgins.”

Four hundred virgins were found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead who had not known a man’s bed. They brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.

They sent messengers to the children of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and instructed the Benjaminites to receive them peacefully. The children of Benjamin came at that time, and wives were given to them from the daughters of Jabesh-gilead; but they found no others whom they could give to them in the same way.

All Israel grieved greatly and repented over the destruction of one tribe of Israel. The elders said: “What shall we do for the survivors who have not received wives? All the women of Benjamin have perished, and we must provide with great care and effort so that one tribe is not wiped out from Israel.

“We cannot give them our daughters, bound as we are by the oath and curse by which we said: ‘Cursed is the one who gives one of his daughters as a wife to Benjamin.’”

They took counsel and said: “Behold, there is an annual solemnity of the Lord at Shiloh, situated north of the city of Bethel, east of the road that runs from Bethel toward Shechem, and south of the town of Lebonah.”

They commanded the children of Benjamin, saying: “Go and lie in wait in the vineyards. When you see the daughters of Shiloh come out, as is customary, to lead the dances, go suddenly out from the vineyards and seize them, each man one wife, and go to the land of Benjamin.

“When their fathers or brothers come and begin to complain against you and quarrel with you, we shall say to them: ‘Be merciful to them. They did not seize them by the right of warriors and conquerors; rather, when they asked to receive them, you did not give them, and the fault is on your side.’”

The children of Benjamin did as they had been commanded. According to their number, they seized for themselves wives from among those who were leading the dances, each man one. They went away to their possession, building cities and living in them.

The children of Israel also returned by tribes and families to their tents. In those days there was no king in Israel, but each person did what seemed right to him.  
**R.** Amen.

**Antiphon 1.** Praise the Lord, for the Lord is kind; sing praise to his name, for it is sweet. Psalm CXXXIV.

[Col. 0436B] **Prayer.** Let us praise you, O Lord, because you are kind and sweet. Grant, therefore, that while we persist in your praise, you may call us away from the enticements of the world or join us to the fellowship of the perfect.  
**R.** Amen.

Through mercy.

**Antiphon 2.** By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, O Zion. Psalm CXXXVI.

**Prayer.** O Lord, our Redeemer, remove our captivity, to which the adversary has consigned us because we wickedly consented to him. As we have sat humbled, weeping beside the rivers of confusion, may you rescue us from temptations and enable us to rise. May unstable pleasure not drag us into the abyss, but may the humility of tears lead us to heaven.  
**R.** Amen.

[Col. 0436C] Through your mercy, O God, etc.

**Antiphon 3.** Be near, O Lord, to those who call upon you, and hear our prayer. Psalm CXLIV.

**R.** Why, O Lord, have you rejected us? Will you be angry forever with us? Will your fury be against the sheep of your flock? Remember your congregation, O Lord, which you created from the beginning.  
**V.** Save your people, O Lord, and bless your inheritance.  
**P.** Which you created.

## At Sext

**Reading from the Prophet Hosea (Chapter V)**

**R.** Thanks be to God.

Hear this, priests, and pay attention, house of Israel; listen, house of the king. For judgment is against you, because you have become a snare for the watchtower and like a net spread over Tabor. You have turned sacrifices aside into the depths, and I am the instructor of them all.

I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me, because now Ephraim has committed fornication; Israel has been defiled. They will not direct their thoughts toward returning to their Lord, because the spirit of fornication is among them, and they have not known the Lord.

The arrogance of Israel will answer to his face. Israel and Ephraim have fallen through their iniquity; Judah too will fall with them.

With their flocks and herds they will go to seek the Lord, but they will not find him, because he has been taken away from them. They have acted treacherously against the Lord, for they have begotten foreign children; now the harvest will devour them together with their parents.

Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; howl in Beth-aven. Behind you, Benjamin! Ephraim will be desolation on the day of corruption. Among the tribes of Israel I have shown faithfulness.

The princes of Judah have become like those who move a boundary marker; upon them I shall pour out my wrath like water. Ephraim is oppressed and is like rot to the house of Judah.

Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his bond. Ephraim went to Assyria and sent to the avenging king, but he will not be able to heal you, nor will he be able to release you from your bond.

For I shall be like a lioness to Ephraim and like a lion’s cub to the house of Judah. I shall seize them and go away; I shall carry them off, and there will be no one to rescue them.

I shall go away and return to my place until you fail and seek my face. In their distress they will rise early to me: “Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has torn us, and he will heal us.”  
**R.** Amen.

## At Vespers

**He made the moon.**  
**V.** A man went out. fol. 178.

**Hymn.**

The Word of the Father, who came forth made flesh,

the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world:

to you we come bowed down, that we may drink

the blood of the life-giving passion.

Show the marks of your sacred wounds.

Let the mighty sign

of the renowned Cross arise,

remaining forever in its strength

and granting salvation to believers.

The reed, the nails, the spittle, the myrrh-like drink,

the crown of thorns, the scourges, the lance—

the blows of condemnation were impressed upon you.

Now, because of these, wipe away all our crimes.

May the fountain of the sacred wound water our inmost hearts;

may the blood wash away the contagions of wickedness.

May the present life be free from every crime;

may the future life be granted as a blessed gift.

So that, when the day of resurrection shines forth

and the glory of the kingdom illumines the world,

we may follow the way of heaven,

which draws us, once received, to become its everlasting inhabitants.

Honor be to the eternal God, glory

to the one Father and to his only Son,

with the Spirit; this Trinity lives forever,

powerful throughout the ages of ages.

Amen.

**Supplication.** Let us pray to the Redeemer of the world, our Lord Jesus Christ; let us beseech him with every supplication that, through the marks of his passion, he may graciously deign to justify us. Kyrie, eleison. Christe, eleison. Kyrie, eleison.

**Capitula.** As we begin, at the appointed return of time, the festival of your passion, Christ, Son of God, with the devout service of our hearts—the passion in which, for our sake, you endured the tongues of persecutors and were crucified by the wounds inflicted by those who betrayed you—we ask and entreat you not to withdraw from us.

Since, as tribulation approaches, there is no one to help, may you alone raise us up by the aid of your passion. Therefore do not hand us over to our enemies for evil, but receive your servants for good, so that the proud who accuse us—the enemies, namely, of our souls—may be driven away by the power of your strength.

For you are the divine lamp, placed through your humanity upon the lampstand of the Cross. Therefore we ask you to set us aflame, lest we come into punishment.

Since you see that we have received the festival of your passion with devoted hearts, make us share in your passion, so that, when the error of our darkness has been dispelled, we may be fortified by the protection of your light.

**Our Father.**

**Humble yourselves for the blessing.**

**Blessing.** May Christ the Lord, whose wounds of passion you receive to be proclaimed with most grateful devotion, make you free from your own passions.  
**R.** Amen.

And may he who wished to be crucified through the flesh he assumed, by the power of his divinity, make you sharers in his kingdom.  
**R.** Amen.

So that in whose passion you have become sorrowful, in his resurrection you may rejoice most fully.  
**R.** Amen.

At the Benedictus. Antiphon. Why have you rejected me, and why do I go about sadly while the enemy afflicts me? Send forth your light and your truth.
