**Response:** Amen.

**Antiphon 3.** “Deliver me, Lord, from the unjust and deceitful man, for you are my God and my strength.”  
**Verse:** “Judge me, God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man.”

**Prayer.** You are our God: deliver us from all the unjust and deceitful, so that, with complete health dwelling in our flesh, we may be worthy to reach the crown appointed for us.

**Response:** Amen.

**Response:** “My sighs are many, Lord, and my heart is mourning. [304] Because you have brought the day of your consolation upon me. My enemies heard of my misfortune.”  
**Petition:** “And they rejoiced. Harvest them as you harvested me, because I groan and there is no one to console me.”  
**Verse:** “All who used to glorify me despised me; for they saw my disgrace.”  
**Petition:** “And they rejoiced with me.”

[Col. 0518A] **Prayer.** God, who see us becoming sorrowful in our trial, give us your most powerful help in the victory of the holy Cross, so that we who, following your example, strive to overcome the world may be worthy after our departure to possess the heavens.

**Antiphon.** “Give joy and gladness to my hearing, Lord, so that the humbled bones may rejoice.”  
**Psalm L.**

**Prayer.** We cry out to you, Lord; have mercy on us. Heal our souls, for we have sinned against you. It is yours to have mercy upon us and to prolong mercy; it is yours to care for the wounds of the soul, not to inflict the deserved vengeance upon revealed crimes, nor to repay [Col. 0518B] thereafter a punishment proportionate to them. Give us the humility that you may regard with favor, and receive our confession, so that you may forgive our sins.

**Response:** Amen.

**Antiphon.** “I have become a laughingstock all day long, and everyone mocks me.”

**Canticle.** “You have seduced me, Lord.” Folio 276.

**Prayer.** Make us, Lord our God, so that we may not grow weary in the mockery of our enemies or the taunting of those who oppose us. But you, who are our defense, deliver us from the contradiction of the wicked.

**Response:** Amen.

**Antiphon.** “Make me hear your mercy in the morning, for I have hoped in you, Lord.”  
**Petition:** “Show me the way by which I should walk, for to you, [Col. 0518C] Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”  
**Verse:** “Praise the Lord with tambourine and choir; praise him with strings and organ.”

**Reading from the Book of Samuel (Second Book of Kings II).**

**Response:** Thanks be to God.

In those days: Abner, son of Ner and commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, led him around through the camps, and established him as king over Gilead, Geshur, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel. Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for two years. Only the house of Judah followed David.

The number of days that David dwelt as ruler in Hebron [Col. 0518D] over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.

Abner, son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, went out from the camp toward the pool of Gibeon. Joab, son of Zeruiah, and David’s servants also went out and met them beside the pool of Gibeon. When they had come together, they sat facing one another, these on one side of the pool and those on the other.

Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men rise and play before us.” Joab replied, “Let them rise.” So twelve men from Benjamin, on the side of Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, and twelve of David’s servants rose.

Each man seized the head of his companion, drove his sword into the side of his opponent, and they fell together. Therefore that place was called “The Field of the Strong,” at Gibeon.

A very fierce battle arose on that day, [Col. 0519A] and Abner and the men of Israel were exhausted before the servants of David. Three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was an exceedingly swift runner, like one of the wild goats that dwell in the forests.

Asahel pursued Abner and did not turn aside to the right or to the left, but continued pursuing Abner. Abner looked behind him and said, “Are you Asahel?” He replied, “I am.”

Abner said to him, “Turn either to the right or to the left, seize one of the young men, and take his armor for yourself.” But Asahel refused to stop pursuing him.

Again Abner said to Asahel, “Withdraw; do not follow me, lest I be forced to strike you through to the ground, and I would not be able to lift my face before your brother Joab.” But he scorned to listen and refused to turn aside.

Therefore Abner struck him in the groin with the butt of his spear, piercing him, and he died [Col. 0519B] there. All who passed by the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped there.

As Joab and Abishai pursued the fleeing Abner, the sun set. They came to the hill of the aqueduct, which is opposite the valley and the road to the wilderness at Gibeon. The sons of Benjamin gathered around Abner and formed themselves into a single band; they stood at the top of a hill.

Abner called out to Joab and said, “Will your [305] sword rage forever toward slaughter? Do you not know that despair is dangerous? How long will you not tell the people to stop pursuing their brothers?”

Joab said, “As the Lord lives, if you had spoken earlier, the people would have withdrawn in the morning from pursuing [Col. 0519C] their brother.”

So Joab sounded the trumpet, and the whole army stopped. They pursued Israel no further and did not continue the battle.

Abner and his men went through the plain throughout that entire night. They crossed the Jordan, passed through all Beth-horon, and came to the camp.

Joab returned, having abandoned the pursuit of Abner, and gathered all the people. Nineteen of David’s servants were missing, besides Asahel. But David’s servants had struck down three hundred and sixty men of Benjamin and of those who had been with Abner, and they died.

They took Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father at Bethlehem.

**Response:** Amen.

## At Terce

### Jesus son of Sirach (*Ecclesiasticus*, chapter VIII)

My son, do not judge against a judge, for he judges according to what is just [Col. 0520A]. Do not go along the road with a reckless man, lest perhaps he heap his troubles upon you; for he goes according to his own will, and you will perish together with his foolishness. Do not quarrel with an angry man, and do not go into the desert with a reckless man, for blood is as nothing before him, and where there is no help, he will strike you down. Do not take counsel with fools, for they cannot love anything except what pleases them. Do not take counsel in the presence of a stranger, for you do not know what he may bring forth. Do not reveal your heart to everyone, lest perhaps he bring you a favor and then reproach you.

My son, if you pay attention to me, you will learn; and if you apply your mind, you will become wise. If you incline your ear, you will receive instruction; and if you love listening, you will become wise.

[Col. 0520B] **Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, chapter III)**

**R.** Thanks be to God.

In those days, when there was war between the house of Saul and the house of David, Abner son of Ner ruled the house of Saul. Saul had had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, and Abner went in to her. Ish-bosheth said to Abner, “Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?”

He was exceedingly angry because of Ish-bosheth’s words and said: “Am I a dog’s head belonging to Judah today, that I should have shown mercy to the house of Saul your father, and to his brothers and his relatives, and should not have delivered you into the hands of David—and today you question me concerning a woman, as though I were to be reproached?” May God do this to Abner and add this also [Col. 0520C], unless, just as the Lord swore to David, so I shall do with him: that the kingdom may be transferred from the house of Saul and that David’s throne may be raised over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.

He could not answer him anything, because he feared him.

Therefore Abner sent messengers to David at Hebron on his behalf, saying: “Whose is the land?” And he said that they should speak thus: “Make an alliance with me, and my hand will be with you, and I will bring all Israel over to you.”

David said: “Do not be afraid. I will make an alliance with you, but I ask one thing of you: you shall not see my face before you bring me Michal, daughter of Saul; then you may come and see me.”

David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, son of Saul, saying: “Restore to me my wife Michal, [Col. 0520D] whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”

So Ish-bosheth sent for her and took her away from her husband, Phaltiel son of Laish. Her husband followed her, weeping as far as Bahurim. Abner said to him: “Go and return.” And he returned.

Abner also spoke to the elders of Israel, saying: “Yesterday and the day before, you were seeking David to reign over you. Now, then, act, for the Lord has spoken to David, saying: ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from all their enemies.’”

Abner also spoke to Benjamin. He went to speak to David at Hebron about everything that was pleasing to Israel and to all Benjamin. Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, and David made a feast for Abner and [306] the men who had come with him [Col. 0521A].

Abner said to David: “I will rise and gather all Israel to my lord the king; I will make a covenant with you, and you shall rule over all, as your soul desires.”

When David had escorted Abner and Abner was departing in peace, David’s servants immediately arrived, as did Joab, after striking down the raiders, with very great spoil. Abner was no longer with David in Hebron, because David had already dismissed him and he had departed in peace.

Joab and all the army that was with him arrived afterward. Joab was told by those who reported it: “Abner son of Ner came to the king, and he dismissed him, and he departed in peace.”

Joab entered the king and said: “What have you done? Behold, Abner came to you; why did you dismiss him, and why has he gone away? Do you not know Abner son of Ner, that he came for this purpose: to deceive you, to learn your departure and your entrance, and to know everything that you do?”

Joab then went out from David, sent messengers after Abner, and brought him back from the cistern of Sirah, without David’s knowledge. When Abner had returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the middle of the gate, as though to speak with him deceitfully; and he struck him there in the groin, and he died in vengeance for the blood of his brother Asahel.

When David heard of what had happened, he said: “I and my kingdom are innocent before God forever of the blood of Abner son of Ner.” **R.** Amen.

**R.** Amen.

## At Sext

### Reading from the Book of the Prophet Jeremiah (chapter II)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0522C] Thus says the Lord: “Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What injustice did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me, walked after vanity, and became vain? They did not say: ‘Where is the Lord, who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness, through an uninhabited [307] and trackless land, through a land of thirst and the image of death, and through a land in which no man walked and no human being dwelt?’

“Then I brought you into the land of Carmel, so that you might eat its fruit and its good things. But when you entered, you defiled my land and made my inheritance an abomination. The priests did not say: ‘Where is the Lord?’ Those who held the law did not know me, and the shepherds transgressed against me. [Col. 0522D] The prophets prophesied by Baal, and they followed idols.

“Therefore I will still contend with you in judgment, says the Lord, and I will dispute with your children. Cross over to the islands of Kittim and see; send to Kedar and consider carefully, and see whether anything like this has happened: whether a nation has changed its gods—and yet they are not gods. But my people have changed their glory for an idol.

“Be astonished, heavens, at this, and let its gates be utterly desolate, says the Lord. For my people have done two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water.

“Is Israel a slave or a household servant? Why, then, has he become a prey? [Col. 0523A] Lions roared over him; they uttered their voice, they made his land a desolation. His cities have been burned, and there is no one who dwells in them. The children of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you to the crown of your head.

“Has this not happened to you because you abandoned the Lord your God at the time when he was leading you on the way? And now, what do you want on the road to Egypt, to drink turbid water? And what have you to do with the road of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river?

“Your wickedness will rebuke you, and your apostasy will reproach you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to have abandoned the Lord your God, and that the fear of him is not in you, says the Lord God of hosts.

“From ancient times you broke my yoke and tore my bonds, and you said: ‘I will not serve.’ For on every high hill and under every leafy tree you lay down like a prostitute.

“But I planted you as a chosen vine, wholly true seed.” **R.** Amen.

## At None

### Jesus son of Sirach (*Ecclesiasticus*, chapter X)

Every authority has a short life. A prolonged illness burdens the physician. The physician cuts short a brief illness; so too, a king exists today and will die tomorrow. For when a human being dies, he will inherit serpents, beasts, and worms.

The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God, for his heart has withdrawn from the one who made him [Col. 0524B]. [308] The beginning of every sin is pride; whoever clings to it will be filled with curses, and it will overthrow him in the end.

Therefore the Lord dishonored the assemblies of the wicked, and he destroyed them to the end. God destroyed the seats of proud leaders and made the humble sit in their place. God dried up the roots of proud nations and planted the humble from among those nations.

The Lord overturned the lands of the nations and destroyed them to their foundations. He dried them up, dispersed them, and caused their memory to cease from the earth. God destroyed the memory of the proud and left the memory of the humble in understanding.

**R.** Amen.

### Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, chapter III)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0524C] In those days David said: “I and my kingdom are innocent before God forever of the blood of Abner son of Ner. May it come upon the head of Joab and upon all the house of his father. May there never cease from the house of Joab one who suffers from a discharge, or is a leper, or holds a spindle, or falls by the sword, or lacks bread.”

Thus Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel at Gibeon in battle.

David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him: “Tear your garments, gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before the funeral of Abner.” King David himself followed the bier.

When they had buried Abner in Hebron, King David raised his voice and wept over Abner’s [Col. 0524D] grave; all the people also wept. As the king mourned and lamented Abner, he said: “Abner did not die as worthless men usually die. Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not weighed down with fetters; but just as men fall before the children of iniquity, so you have fallen.”

All the people wept over him again and again.

When the whole multitude came to eat with David while it was still daylight, David swore, saying: “May God do this to me and add this also, if I taste bread or anything else before sunset.”

All the people heard, and everything the king did in the sight of all the people pleased them. The whole populace and all Israel knew on that day that the king had not arranged for Abner son of Ner to be killed.

The king also said [Col. 0525A] to his servants: “Do you not know that a great leader has fallen today in Israel? I am still tender and an anointed king, but these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too harsh for me. May the Lord repay the one who does evil according to his wickedness.”

### Chapter IV

Ish-bosheth son of Saul heard that Abner had fallen in Hebron, and his hands were weakened, and all Israel was disturbed.

There were two men, commanders of raiders, belonging to the son of Saul. The name of one was Baanah and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the sons of Benjamin. For Beeroth also was reckoned among Benjamin. The Beerothites fled to Gittaim and lived there as resident aliens until that time.

Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was disabled in his feet. He was five years old when the messenger came from Saul and Jonathan from Jezreel. [Col. 0525B] His nurse took him and fled; but, while she hurried to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.

The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came and entered the house of Ish-bosheth during the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon. The woman who guarded the door of the house, cleaning wheat, had fallen asleep.

They entered the house secretly, carrying ears of wheat, and Rechab and his brother Baanah struck him in the groin and fled. When they had entered the house, he was sleeping on his bed in the inner chamber; they struck him and killed him. They took his head and went by the road through the wilderness all night, and brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron.

They said to the king: “Behold the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your [Col. 0525C] life. Today the Lord has given my lord the king vengeance upon Saul and his offspring.”

David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them: “As the Lord lives, who has rescued my life from every distress, when the one who announced to me and said, ‘Saul is dead,’ thought that he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag—the reward I ought to have given him for his message—how much more now, when wicked men have killed an innocent man in his own house, upon his bed? Shall I not require his blood from your hand and remove you from the land?”

David therefore commanded his servants, and they killed them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung them over the pool in Hebron. [Col. 0525D] But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron.

### Chapter V

All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron, saying: “[309] Behold, we are your bone and your flesh. Yesterday and the day before, when Saul was king over us, you were the one leading Israel out and bringing it back. The Lord also said to you: ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be leader over Israel.’”

All the elders of Israel also came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the Lord. They anointed David king over Israel.

David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years. In Hebron he reigned over Judah for seven years and six months; in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

The king and all the men who were with him went to Jerusalem [Col. 0526A], to the Jebusite who inhabited the land. They said to David: “You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame,” saying: “David shall not enter here.”

David captured the stronghold of Zion; this is the city of David. For David had promised a reward on that day to anyone who struck down the Jebusite and touched the water pipes of the roof, and removed the blind and the lame who hated David’s life. Therefore it is said in the proverb: “The blind and the lame shall not enter the temple.”

**R.** Amen.

### The Canticle of Job (chapter XIX)

Behold, I cry out, suffering violence, and no one hears;  
I shout, and there is no one who judges.

He has fenced in my path, and I cannot pass;  
and he has placed darkness upon my road.

He has stripped me of my glory  
and taken the crown from my head.

He has destroyed me on every side, and I perish;  
and like a tree torn up by the roots, he has taken away my hope.

His fury has grown angry against me,  
and he has treated me as his enemy.

His raiders have come together and made a way through me;  
they have surrounded my tent in a circle [Col. 0528B].

He has put my brothers far from me,  
and my acquaintances have withdrawn like strangers.

My relatives have abandoned me,  
and those who knew me have forgotten me.

The inhabitants of my house and my maidservants have regarded me as a stranger;  
I was like a foreigner in their eyes.

I called my servant, and he did not answer;  
with my own mouth I pleaded with him.

My wife shuddered at my breath,  
and I pleaded with the children of my womb.

Fools also despised me;  
and when I had withdrawn from them, they slandered me.

My former counselors abhorred me,  
and [Col. 0528C] the one whom I loved most has opposed me.

My bone has clung to my skin and flesh, which have been consumed;  
and only my lips remain around my teeth.

Who will grant me that my words may be written?  
Who will give me that they may be inscribed in a book with an iron stylus,  
and engraved with lead on a plate, or with a chisel upon flint?

For I know that my Redeemer lives,  
and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.

And again I shall be clothed with my skin,  
and in my flesh I shall see the Lord.  
I myself shall see him, and my eyes shall behold him, and no other.  
This hope has been laid up in my bosom,  
and my inheritance is in my God.

## Prayer

We believe, Lord, that in this flesh with which we are clothed [Col. 0528D] we shall see you, and that with our eyes we shall behold you in the glory in which you will judge the world. Therefore make us have the eyes of our inner being opened, so that we may know you in everlasting glory.

**R.** Amen.

### Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, chapter XI)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

At the time when kings usually go forth to war, David sent Joab, his servants with him, and all Israel. They devastated [311] the sons of Ammon and besieged Rabbah [Col. 0529A], while David remained in Jerusalem.

As these things were happening, it came about one day that David rose from his bed after midday and walked upon the roof of the royal house. He saw a woman washing herself on the opposite roof; the woman was exceedingly beautiful.

The king sent and inquired who the woman was. He was told that she was Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

David sent messengers and took her. When she had entered to him, he slept with her; and she was immediately purified from her uncleanness. She returned to her house having conceived. She sent word to David and said: “I have conceived.”

David sent to Joab, saying: “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” Joab sent Uriah to David, and Uriah came to David.

[Col. 0529B] David asked how Joab was doing, and how the people were doing, and how the war was being conducted. David said to Uriah: “Go down to your house and wash your feet.”

Uriah went out from the king’s house, and the king’s food followed him. Uriah slept before the gate of the royal house with the other servants of his lord, and he did not go down to his house.

David was told: “Uriah did not go to his house.” David said to Uriah: “Did you not come from a journey? Why did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David: “The ark of God, Israel, and Judah dwell in tents, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord remain upon the face of the earth. Shall I enter my house to eat and drink and [Col. 0529C] sleep with my wife? By your life and by the life of your soul, I will not do this thing.”

David said to Uriah: “Remain here today also, and tomorrow I will send you away.”

Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next. David called him to eat and drink before him and made him drunk. In the evening he went out and slept on his bed with the servants of his lord, but he did not go down to his house.

When morning came, David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah. He wrote in the letter: “Place Uriah opposite the strongest part of the battle, and withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and die.”

Therefore, while Joab was besieging the city, he placed Uriah where he knew that the strongest men were. The men came out from the city and fought against Joab. Some of the people, David’s servants, fell [Col. 0529D], and Uriah the Hittite also died.

Joab sent word and reported to David all the events of the battle. He commanded the messenger, saying: “When you have finished telling all the words of the battle to the king, if you see that he becomes angry and says: ‘Why did you approach the wall to fight? Did you not know that many missiles would be hurled down from the wall? Who struck Abimelech son of Jerubbaal? Was it not a woman who threw a millstone fragment upon him from the wall and killed him at Thebez? Why did you approach the wall?’—then you shall say: ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.’”

The messenger departed, came, and reported to David everything Joab had commanded him.

The messenger said to David: “The men prevailed against us and came out against us into the field; but we made a charge and pursued [Col. 0530A] them as far as the city gate. The archers directed their arrows at your servants from the wall above, and some of the king’s servants died; moreover, your servant Uriah the Hittite also died.”

David said to the messenger: “Thus you shall say to Joab: ‘Let this matter not trouble you, for the outcome of battle is varied; now the sword consumes this one, now that one. Strengthen your warriors against the city, so that you may destroy it, and encourage them.’”

The wife of Uriah heard that her husband Uriah had died, and she mourned him. When the mourning had ended, David sent for her and brought her into his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But this deed that David had done was displeasing before the Lord.

**R.** Amen.

**Hymn. “The Time of Night.” fol. 257**

Do not delay or be slow; now attend, now turn, now look upon us, so that our prayer—which now turns into our own bosom through remorse for its secret matters—may be directed before your sight by the purified groaning of its heart.

Our Father.

### Ecclesiasticus of Solomon (chapter V)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

My son, do not follow the desire of your heart, and do not say: “How could I have done it?” or “Who will subject me because of my deeds?” For God will surely take vengeance.

Do not say: “I have sinned, and what sad thing has happened to me?” For the Most High is a patient requiter. Concerning a forgiven sin, do not be without fear, and do not add sin upon sin.

Do not say: “The mercy of God is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins.” For mercy and wrath quickly draw near from him, and his wrath looks upon sinners.

Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly [Col. 0530D], and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.

Do not be anxious about unjust riches, for they will profit you nothing on the day of covering and vengeance.

Do not toss yourself about in every wind, and do not go along every road; for thus a sinner is tested with a double tongue.

Stand firm in the way of God, in the truth of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice follow you.

**R.** Amen.

### Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, chapter XII)

**R.** Thanks be to God.

*[The supplied source ends here.]*
In those days: The Lord sent Nathan to David. When he had come to him, he said to him:

“There were two men in one city, one rich and the other poor. The rich man had very many sheep and oxen. But the poor man had nothing at all except one little ewe, which he had bought and nourished. It grew up with him and with his children together, eating of his bread, drinking from his cup, and sleeping in his bosom; and it was like a daughter to him.

[Col. 0531A]

“When a certain traveler came to the rich man, he spared taking from his own sheep and oxen to prepare a feast for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s ewe and prepared food for the man who had come to him.”

David was exceedingly angry against that man, and he said to Nathan: “As the Lord lives, the man who has done this is a son of death. He shall restore the ewe fourfold, because he did this thing and did not spare.”

Nathan then said to David: “You are that man. Thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from the hand of Saul. I gave you your lord’s house and your lord’s wives into your bosom, and I gave you the house of Israel and Judah.

[Col. 0531B] And if these things are too little, I will add to you things much greater.

“‘Why, then, have you despised the word of the Lord, so as to do evil in my sight? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword, took his wife as your wife, and killed him by the sword of the Ammonites. Therefore the sword shall not depart from your house forever, because you have despised me and taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite, so that she might be your wife.

“‘Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will raise evil against you from your own house; I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall sleep with your wives in the sight of this people. For you acted secretly, but I will do this thing in the sight of all Israel, in the sight of the sun.’”

David said to Nathan: “I have sinned against the Lord.”

And Nathan said to David: [Col. 0531C] “The Lord has also taken away your sin; you shall not die. Nevertheless, because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme by this deed, the son who has been born to you shall surely die.”

Then Nathan returned to his house. And the Lord struck the child whom the wife of Uriah had borne to David, and he became gravely ill. David pleaded with the Lord for the child; David fasted with a fast, went inside by himself, and lay on the ground.

The elders of his household came to him and urged him to rise from the ground, but he refused, nor did he eat food with them. On the seventh day the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said: “Behold, while the child was still alive, [Col. 0531D] we spoke to him, and he did not heed our voice; how much more, if we tell him that the child is dead, will he afflict himself?”

When David saw his servants whispering, he understood that the child was dead. He said to his servants: “Is the child dead?” They answered him: “He is dead.”

Then David rose, washed and anointed himself; and when he had changed his clothing, he entered the house of the Lord, worshiped, and returned to his house. He asked that bread be set before him, and he ate.

His servants said to him: “What is this that you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept; but when the child died, you rose and ate bread.”

He replied: “While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said: ‘Who knows whether the Lord may perhaps give him to me [Col. 0532A], and the child may live?’ But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, rather; but he will not return to me.”

David consoled Bathsheba, his wife. He went in to her and slept with her; she bore a son and called his name Solomon, and the Lord loved him. He sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah—“Beloved of the Lord”—because the Lord loved him.

R. Amen.

Antiphon 1. Unjust witnesses rising against me questioned me about things I did not know, repaying me evil for good. With feigned words they gnashed their teeth against me.

V. Judge, O Lord, those who harm me, and fight against those who fight me.

Prayer. [Col. 0532B] Unjust witnesses rising against you, Lord, questioned you about things you did not know. Yet what did you not know, when you had already perceived beforehand the treacheries of those who hated you, and, knowing all future things, knew everything beforehand? Therefore, by the profound mystery of your compassion, you signify that you did not know the blasphemies of those who questioned you. Make us truly know and embrace this mystery, and grant us to recognize with complete faith the mysteries of our redemption, and to declare them known to the enemies who questioned you.

R. Amen.

Antiphon 2. Sinners spoke iniquity on high. They set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passed over the earth. O Lord, in your city you will reduce their image to nothing.

Prayer. [Col. 0532C] On high, Lord, sinners spoke against you, crying out in loud voices while concealing the pride of their hearts. Therefore, let those who strive to set their mouths against you in heaven return to earth, where they may be shattered through repentance, so that, humbly acknowledging you with us as the Son of God, they may not think proudly but may always submit to your admonitions.

R. Amen.

P. And have mercy.

P. Now have mercy.

V. You who redeemed the world by your cross and, becoming the triumphant victor over hell, conquered punishment,

P. Now have mercy.

P. Now have mercy.

Hymn. “O Nazarene.” Folio 144.

Capitulum. To defend the inheritance purchased at the price of your blood, Lord Jesus Christ, take up victorious weapons; rising for our help, arm us with the gifts of faith as with a shield, so that the arrows of the enemy may not pierce our minds. Rather, as our King, cut down the enemy himself with the divine sword. And because you are the salvation of our soul, grant us, we ask, this gift: that with watchful minds we may follow you, and, laying aside the burden of sin, may attain the good things you have promised.

Our Father.

[Col. 0535A]

Prayer. Jesus, our God, who, having made a scourge from cords, drive from your temple those who buy and sell, grant us that in your Church we may neither be seized by the pursuit of temporal gain nor behave within it with sordid morals; but let zeal for your house consume us in such a way that you may present us to our brothers as examples pleasing to you.

R. Amen.

Per.

Antiphon 3. Deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy, and protect me, O Lord, from the assembly of the malicious.

R. Hear my prayer, O God, when I am troubled; deliver my soul from the fear of the enemy.

Prayer. [Col. 0535B] Deliver my soul, O Lord, from the fear of the enemy, and rescue it from the assembly of the malicious, so that the soul which was drawn out of the pit of misery by the wound of your Passion may, believing in you, be led to the freedom of eternal glory.

R. Amen.

Per.

R. I have become a mockery and a reproach to all my people; I have been filled with bitterness and drunk with wormwood. My entrails have been poured out, and I said: “I am lost.” See, O Lord, and judge the cause of my soul.

P. Defender of my life.

R. Destroy my enemies who afflict my soul.

P. Defender.

Prayer. Remember, Jesus, the wormwood and gall with which you were offered a bitter drink for the ungodly. Therefore, we ask, let your bitterness be our perpetual sweetness [Col. 0535C], so that in that very thing in which you willingly became bitter for us, we may rejoice happily, both here and forever.

R. Amen.

Per.

## At Lauds

Antiphon. Give joy and gladness to my hearing, O Lord, so that the humbled bones may rejoice. Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Psalm 50.

Prayer. “This psalm.” Folio 173.

Antiphon. Whatever I have vowed, I shall repay to you, my Savior and Lord.

### Canticle of Jonah (Chapter II)

I cried to the Lord my God in my tribulation,  
* and he heard my cry from the belly of hell.

[Col. 0535D]

You heard my voice;  
* you cast me into the height of the heart of the sea, and the streams surrounded me.

All your heights and your waves passed over me.  
* And I said: “I have been cast away from your eyes; perhaps I shall not again turn to look upon your holy temple.”

The waters closed over me, even to my soul;  
* the abyss surrounded me;

the deep covered my head.  
* At last my head sank into the clefts of the mountains.

I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints;  
* and may my life rise from corruption to you, Lord my God.

[Col. 0536A]

When my soul was failing within me, I remembered the Lord my God;

and my prayer shall come  
* to your holy temple.

Those who attend to vain and false things  
* have abandoned your mercy.

But I will sacrifice to you with the voice of praise and confession;  
* I will repay what I vowed, a sacrifice to my Savior and Lord.

Prayer. Our Savior and Lord, make us vow a vow to you with a pure heart, so that, while observing your commandments in an unwearied course, we may patiently endure all present adversities.

R. Amen.

Per.

Matutinarium. I shall sing and understand in the morning, because you will come to me.

R. I shall sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.

Lauda. Praise the Lord in his holy places; praise him with psaltery and harp. Psalm 150.

[Col. 0536B]

Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, Chapter XV).

R. Thanks be to God.

In those days: Absalom prepared for himself chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. Rising early, Absalom stood beside the entrance of the gate, on the road. Every man who had a case and was coming to the king’s judgment he called to himself and said: “From what city are you?”

He answered: “I am your servant from one of the tribes of Israel.”

Absalom replied: “Your words seem good and just to me, but no one has been appointed by the king [Col. 0536C] to hear you.” And Absalom said: “Who will appoint me judge over the land, so that all who have a case may come to me and I may judge justly?”

Whenever a man approached him to greet him, he extended his hand, took hold of him, and kissed him. He did this to every Israelite who came for judgment to be heard by the king, and he stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

After forty years, Absalom said to King David: “I will go and fulfill the vows I have vowed to the Lord in Hebron. For your servant made a vow when I was in Geshur of Syria, saying: ‘If the Lord brings me back to Jerusalem, I will sacrifice to the Lord.’”

King David said to him: “Go in peace.” He rose and went to Hebron.

Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes [Col. 0536D] of Israel, saying: “As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, say: ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron.’”

Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom, summoned and going with a simple heart, knowing nothing of the affair. Absalom also summoned Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city of Giloh. While he was offering sacrifices, the conspiracy grew strong, and the people, running together, increased with Absalom.

A messenger came to David, saying: “All Israel follows Absalom with its whole heart.”

David said to his servants who were with him in Jerusalem: “Rise, let us flee; for there will be no escape for us from the face of Absalom. Hurry to depart, lest he come upon us, drive ruin upon us, and strike the city with the edge of the sword.”

The king’s servants said to him: “Whatever our lord the king commands, we, your servants, gladly carry out.”

[Col. 0537A]

The king therefore went out, and all his household on foot. The king left ten concubines to guard the house. The king and all Israel went out on foot and stood some distance from the house. All his servants walked beside him, and the battalions of the Cherethites and Pelethites, together with all the warriors from Gath—six hundred men who had followed him from Gath on foot—went before the king.

The king said to Ittai the Gittite: “Why are you coming with us? Return and dwell with the king, for you are a foreigner and have departed from your own place. Yesterday you came, and today you are compelled to go out with us? I am going where I am going. Return and take your brothers back with you, and may the Lord show you mercy and truth [Col. 0537B], because you have shown grace and faithfulness.”

Ittai answered the king: “As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether in death or in life, there also shall your servant be.”

David said to Ittai: “Come and cross over.” Ittai the Gittite crossed over, as did the king, all the men who were with him, and the rest of the multitude. Everyone wept with a loud voice, and all the people crossed over. The king himself crossed the Kidron torrent, and all the people proceeded toward the road of the olive trees, which looks toward the desert.

Zadok the priest came, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar went up until all the people who had departed from the [Col. 0537C] city had finished crossing.

The king said to Zadok: “Carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and show me it and his tabernacle. But if he says to me, ‘You do not please me,’ here I am; let him do what is good in his sight.”

The king also said to Zadok the priest: “O seer, return to the city in peace, and let Achimaas your son and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, your two sons, be with you. Behold, I shall hide in the plains of the desert until word comes from you to inform me.”

So Zadok and Abiathar carried the ark of God back to Jerusalem and remained there.

David was climbing the slope of the Mount of Olives, ascending and weeping, walking barefoot and with his head covered. All the people who were with him also ascended with covered heads, weeping.

David was informed that Ahithophel was among the conspiracy with Absalom. David said: “I beg you, Lord, thwart the counsel of Ahithophel.”

When David reached the summit of the mountain where he was going to worship the Lord, behold, Hushai the Archite came to meet him, with torn clothing and dust covering his [Col. 0537D] head.

David said to him: “If you come with me, you will be a burden to me. But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘I am your servant, O king; let me live. As I was your father’s servant, so I shall be your servant,’ you will frustrate the counsel of Ahithophel.

“You have Zadok and Abiathar the priests with you. Every word that you hear in the king’s house, report to Zadok and Abiathar the priests. For their two sons are with them: Achimaas, the son of Zadok, and Jonathan, the son of Abiathar. Through them you shall send me every word that you hear.”

So Hushai, David’s friend, came into the city [Col. 0538A], and Absalom also entered Jerusalem, with Ahithophel.

### Chapter XVI

When David had crossed a little beyond the summit of the mountain, Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, appeared to meet him with two donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves, one hundred bunches of raisins, one hundred cakes of pressed figs, and two skins of wine.

The king said to Ziba: “What do these things mean?”

Ziba answered: “My lord the king: The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride; the bread and cakes are for your servants to eat; and the wine is for anyone who becomes exhausted in the desert to drink.”

The king said: “Where is your lord’s son?”

Ziba answered the king: [Col. 0538B] “He remained in Jerusalem, saying: ‘Today the house of Israel will restore my father’s kingdom to me.’”

The king said to Ziba: “All that belonged to Mephibosheth is yours.”

Ziba said: “I beg that I may find favor with you, my lord the king.”

King David came as far as Bahurim. Behold, a man from the family of the house of Saul, named Shimei the son of Gera, came out from there. He proceeded, cursing and throwing stones at David and at all the servants of King David. All the people and all the warriors walked on the king’s right and left.

Thus Shimei spoke while cursing the king: “Go away, go away, man of blood, man of Belial! The Lord has repaid you for all the blood of the house of Saul, because you seized the kingdom in his place. The Lord has given the kingdom into the hand of Absalom your son, and behold, your evils press upon you, because you are a man of blood.”

Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king: “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go and cut off his head.”

The king said: [Col. 0538C] “What have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Let him curse, because the Lord has commanded him to curse David. And who is there who would dare say, ‘Why has he done this?’”

The king said to Abishai and all his servants: “Behold, my son, who came forth from my body, seeks my life; how much more may this son of Benjamin curse me? Leave him, let him curse, according to the Lord’s command. Perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction, and the Lord will repay me good for this cursing today.”

David and his companions continued along the road [Col. 0538D]. Shimei walked along the mountain ridge opposite him, cursing, throwing stones at him, and scattering dust.

The king and all the people who were with him arrived exhausted, and there they refreshed themselves. Absalom and all his people entered Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.

R. Amen.

Hymn. “The Time of Night.” Folio 257.

Capitulum. Attend and hear us, Lord, whom the adversity of the raging enemy troubles and the crushing force of the persecutor harasses; so that, while you see rebellious minds raging against us, you may make us courageous and gird us with unconquered strength.

Our Father.

[Col. 0539A]

Lauda. I have practiced judgment and justice, O Lord; do not hand me over to those who persecute me.

V. Receive your servant for good, so that the proud may not slander me.

Prayer. Teach us to practice judgment and justice, Lord, so that we may trample down the slanders of the proud. Receive your servants for good, because they hope in your salvation. Make those whose inward eyes await the kingdom of your Christ share in the fellowship of the Elect.

R. Amen. Per.

## At Terce

Reading from the Book of Ecclesiastes of Solomon (Chapter VII).

R. Thanks be to God.

[Col. 0539B]

Son, wisdom strengthened the wise man more than ten rulers of a city. For there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin. Do not apply your heart to all the words that are spoken, lest perhaps you hear your servant cursing you; for your conscience knows that you yourself have often cursed others. Slander troubles the wise man and destroys the strength of his heart. The end of a prayer is better than its beginning. Do not be quick to anger, for anger rests in the bosom of a fool. Do not say: “What do you think is the reason that former times were better than they are now?” Such a question is foolish. Wisdom is more useful with wealth, and it benefits those who see the sun more greatly. For just as wisdom protects, so does money. Consider the works of God, for no one can correct the one whom he has despised. On a good day, enjoy good things.

R. Amen.

Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, Chapter XVI).

[Col. 0539C]

R. Thanks be to God.

In those days: When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, had come to Absalom, he said to him: “Hail, O king.”

Absalom said to him: “Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why did you not go with your friend?”

Hushai answered Absalom: “Not at all, for I shall belong to him whom the Lord, all this people, and all Israel have chosen; with him I shall remain. But to say even this: whom shall I serve? Is it not the king’s son? As I obeyed your father, so shall I obey you.”

Absalom said to Ahithophel: “Take counsel about what we should do.”

Ahithophel said to Absalom: “Go in to your father’s concubines, whom he left to guard the house, so that when all Israel hears that you have defiled your father, their hands may be strengthened with you.”

So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof [Col. 0539D], and he went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel. The counsel of Ahithophel, which he gave in those days, was as though someone were consulting God; such was the counsel of Ahithophel, both when he was with David and when he was with Absalom.

### Chapter XVII

Ahithophel therefore said to Absalom: “Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will rise and pursue David this night. I will fall upon him—for he is weary and his hands are weakened—and strike him. When all the people who are with him have fled, I will strike the king when he is alone. I will bring back all the people to you, as one usually returns; for you seek only [Col. 0540A] one man, and all the people shall be at peace.”

His words pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel. Absalom said: “Call Hushai the Archite, and let us hear what he also says.”

When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him: “Ahithophel has spoken in this manner. Should we do it or not? What counsel do you give?”

Hushai said to Absalom: “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai continued: “You know your father and the men who are with him: they are very brave and bitter in spirit, like a bear raging in the forest when her cubs have been taken. Your father is also a warrior, and he will not lodge with the people. Perhaps he is now hiding in pits or in whatever place he has chosen. And when one of them falls at the beginning, anyone who hears it will say: ‘A slaughter has occurred among the people who follow Absalom.’

“Then every brave man whose heart is like a lion’s will melt with fear, for all Israel knows that your father is a strong man and that all who are with him are valiant.

“But this seems to me the right counsel: Let all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as countless as the sand of the sea, and you shall be in their midst.

[Col. 0540B] Let us fall upon him wherever he is found, and cover him as dew falls upon the ground. We shall not leave even one of the men who are with him.

“And if he has entered some city, all Israel shall surround that city with ropes, and we shall drag it into the torrent, so that not even a pebble may be found from it [Col. 0540C].”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said: “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” But by the Lord’s command the useful counsel of Ahithophel was thwarted, so that the Lord might bring evil upon Absalom.

Hushai said to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: “Ahithophel gave Absalom and the elders of Israel this and this counsel, and I gave this and this counsel. Now therefore send quickly and announce to David, saying: ‘Do not remain tonight in the plains of the desert, but cross over without delay, lest the king and all the people who are with him be swallowed up.’”

Jonathan and Achimaas were standing beside the spring of Rogel. A maidservant went and announced it to them. They departed to report the message to King David, for they could not be seen or enter the city.

A certain boy saw them and reported it to Absalom. But they entered quickly into the house of a man in Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they descended into it.

[Col. 0540D]

The woman took a covering and spread it over the mouth of the well, as though she were drying parched grain; and so the matter remained hidden.

When Absalom’s servants came into the house, they said to the woman: “Where are Achimaas and Jonathan?”

The woman answered them: “They passed on quickly, after tasting a little water.”

Those who were searching, finding nothing, returned to Jerusalem. After they had gone, the men came up from the well, went on, and announced to King David: “Rise and cross the river quickly, for Ahithophel has given such counsel against you.”

David and all the people who were with him rose and crossed the Jordan [Col. 0541A] until dawn, before the matter was disclosed; not even one person remained who did not cross the river.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel had not been followed, he saddled his donkey, rose, and went to his house and to his city. Having put his house in order, he hanged himself and died; and he was buried in the tomb of his father.

R. Amen.

Antiphon 1. My enemies have spoken evil against me: “When will he die, and his name perish?” But you, O Lord, have mercy on me.

V. Together they devised evil against me. “Glory” is not said.

Prayer. [Col. 0541B] Your enemies, Lord, desiring to erase your name from the earth, spoke evil about you, saying: “When will he die?”—wishing, that is, to destroy the Christian name. But you, Lord, whose faithful promise we hold—that you remain with us until the end of the age—have mercy on us and raise us up because of the innocence of the faith by which we believe in you, so that the insatiable enemy may not rejoice over us.

R. Amen.

Antiphon 2. Zeal for your house, O Lord, has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me. But as for me, my prayer is to you, O Lord.

V. In the abundance of your mercy, hear me, in the truth of your salvation.

Prayer. Christ, Son of God, whom zeal for the house of God—that is, of your Father—consumed when you boldly drove those who acted wickedly from it with a cord [Col. 0541C], free us from the cord of every iniquity, and grant that we may dwell worthily in the midst of your house, so that we, having ourselves become a spiritual house for you, may deserve to be crowned by you in heaven.

R. Amen.

Antiphon 3. Send forth your hand from on high, O Lord; rescue me and deliver me from the hand of those who are foreign.

V. Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is the right hand of iniquity.

R. All my friends have forgotten me, and the one whom I loved handed me over to those lying in wait for me. Striking me with a cruel wound and terrible eyes, he gave me vinegar to drink. Now, O God, place healing upon my wound.

P. And raise me up.

V. The one who ate my bread has greatly increased his treachery against me; but you, O Lord, have mercy on me.

P. And raise me up.

Prayers. [Col. 0541D] True and merciful God,

P. Have mercy on the orphan who pleads.

V. You who redeem the world by the shedding of blood and the wound of slaughter,

P. Have mercy on the one who pleads.

V. Through the blood of the cross and death, you saved the world by your sacred wound,

P. Have mercy on the one who pleads.

V. By the glory of the cross you dissolve the punishment of Tartarus; save those who believe, O Lord,

P. Have mercy on the one who pleads.

V. May the mystery of the cross bring advancement to all whom you redeemed in the world,

P. Have mercy on the one who pleads.

Hymn. “O Nazarene.” Folio 144.

Capitulum. Have mercy on us, O God, have mercy on us, and hear those who trust in you. Shatter the weapons of those who oppose us; destroy the snares prepared for us, so that, surrounded [Col. 0542A] by heavenly brightness, we may not fall into the pit of death, but with a prepared heart may exalt your merciful truth among the nations—you who endured the reproach of the cross for us.

Our Father.

## At Sext

Reading from the Book of Amos (Chapter V).

R. Thanks be to God.

Seek the Lord, and live; lest perhaps he consume the house of Joseph like fire, and it devour it, with no one to extinguish Bethel. You who turn judgment into wormwood and abandon justice in the land; who make Arcturus and Orion, who turn morning into darkness and change day into night; who summon the waters of the sea and pour them over the face of the earth—the Lord is his name. Who smiles [reading uncertain] at devastation against the strong and brings ruin upon the mighty. They hated the one who rebuked at the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke uprightly. Therefore, because you plundered the poor and took the choice spoil from him, you shall build houses of hewn stone, but you shall not dwell in them; you shall plant delightful vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine. For I know your many crimes and your grievous sins: enemies of the just who accept bribes and oppress the poor at the gate. Therefore the prudent person will keep silent at that time, because it is an evil time. Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and the Lord, God of hosts, will be. [Col. 0542B] R. Amen.

Antiphon 1. Those who sat at the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang against me. [Col. 0542C] But I prayed to you, O Lord. V. My enemies spoke evil against me: “When will he die, and his name perish?”

Prayer. Christ our King, who endured harsh insults on behalf of the ungodly, while the whole unbelieving crowd, drunk with the wine of malice, attacked you at the gate: cleanse us by continual mercy from every contagion of sin, and glorify us by the effectiveness of virtuous action, so that at the end of our life we may not be put to shame when our enemies speak against us at the gate; but, through the encounter of the holy angels, may we be raised up to everlasting joy. R. Amen.

Antiphon 2. In your justice deliver me, O Lord; incline your ear to me; hasten to rescue me. V. In you, O Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be put to shame forever. In your justice deliver me and rescue me.

[Col. 0542D] Prayer. Deliver us, O Lord, in your justice, and incline your ear to our prayer, so that, rescued from evils and refreshed by heavenly things, we may rejoice that we are clothed with eternal immortality. 320 R. Amen.

Antiphon 3. Hear the voice of my prayer when I pray to you, O Lord; when I raise my hands toward your holy temple. V. Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting of my hands an evening sacrifice.

R. Attend to my prayer, O Lord, for I have been greatly humbled. V. Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name. P. For I have been greatly humbled.

Prayers. We do penance for our evils. P. You, Christ, have mercy; we have sinned. V. You who were led like a sheep to the slaughter, O Lord, mercifully protect us. P. You, Christ. V. You who suffered the cross and were enclosed in the tomb, save us from vices. P. You, Christ. V. You before whom the earth trembled when you died on the cross, look upon us who tremble. P. You, Christ. V. Grant that, buried with you in death, O Lord, we may live forever. P. You, Christ.

Hymn. “O Nazarene.” fol. 144.

Prayer. Save your people, O Lord, by your right hand; and you who gave those who fear you the sign of the Cross, grant them the fullest dignity of faith, so that those whom you had rejected when they sinned, you may receive when they turn back. Grant also the necessary help in tribulation, you who became the price for sinners; and yourself reduce the enemy who afflicts us to nothing; yourself bring the redeemed into the city of your surrounding protection. [Col. 0543B] R. Amen.

At None.

Reading from the Book of Ecclesiasticus of Solomon (Chapter XXXVIII).

R. Thanks be to God.

Son, shed tears for the dead, and, as though you had suffered dreadful things, begin to mourn; according to judgment, cover his body, and do not neglect his burial. But because of his passing, bitterly bear his mourning for one day, and console yourself because of the sorrow; and mourn according to his merit for one day, or two because of the reproach. For death hastens because of sorrow, and covers strength, and grief of heart bends the neck. In captivity sorrow remains, and the substance of the poor is according to his heart. Do not give your heart over to sorrow, [Col. 0543C] but drive it away from you; and remember the last things, do not forget them. For there is no return, and you will profit him nothing, while you make yourself worse. Remember my judgment, for so yours also will be. Yesterday for me, and today for you. In the resting-place of the dead, grant his memory rest, and console him at the departure of his spirit. God created medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not reject it. Is not bitter water sweetened by wood? The Most High gave human beings knowledge of the power of these things, so that he might be honored in his wonders. R. Amen.

Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, Chapter XVIII).

R. Thanks be to God.

In those days: When David had reviewed his people, he appointed over them tribunes and centurions, and divided the people into three parts: one third under the command of Joab, one third under the command of Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and one third under the command of Ittai, who was from Gath. And the king said to the people, “I too will go out with you.” But the people answered, “You shall not go out. For if we flee, they will not care greatly about us; and if half of us fall, they will not care enough, because you alone are counted as ten thousand of us. It is therefore better that you remain in the city as our support.” The king said to them, “What seems right to you, I will do.” So the king stood beside the gate, while the people went out by their companies, hundreds and thousands. And the king commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, “Preserve the boy Absalom for me.” And all the people heard the king commanding all the leaders concerning Absalom. [Col. 0544A] Thus the people went out into the field against Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim. The people of Israel were struck down there by David’s army, and a great slaughter occurred on that day, twenty thousand men. The battle there was scattered over the face of the whole land, and the forest consumed far more of the people than the sword devoured on that day.

It happened that Absalom encountered David’s servants while riding a mule. When the mule entered beneath a dense and great oak, his head caught in the oak; and as he hung between heaven and earth, the mule on which he was riding passed on. Someone saw this and reported to Joab, saying, “I saw Absalom hanging from an oak.” Joab said to the man who had reported it, “If you saw him, why did you not strike him to the ground? I would have given you ten shekels of silver and one belt.” He replied to Joab, “Even if you weighed a thousand shekels of silver in my hands, I would never lay my hand on the king’s son; for we heard the king command you, Abishai, and Ittai, saying, ‘Keep the boy Absalom for me.’ And even if I had acted recklessly against my own life, this could never have been hidden from the king, and you would have stood against me.” Joab said, “I will not do as you wish; rather, I shall attack him in your sight.” So Joab took three spears in his hand and thrust them into Absalom’s heart. While he was still quivering, hanging in the oak, ten young men, Joab’s armor-bearers, ran up and struck him and killed him.

Then Joab sounded the trumpet and restrained the people from pursuing the fleeing Israelites, wishing to spare the multitude. And they took Absalom and threw him into the forest, into a great pit, and piled a very large heap of stones over him. All Israel fled to their tents. Absalom had erected a monument for himself while he was still alive in the King’s Valley, for he had said, “I have no son,” and “This will be a memorial of my name.” He had called the monument by his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Hand to this day.

Achimaas son of Zadok said, “I will run and report to the king, because God has judged him from the hand of his enemies.” Joab said to him, “You will not be the messenger today; you shall report on another day. Today I do not want you to report, for the king’s son is dead.” Joab said to Cushi, “Go and report to the king what you have seen.” Cushi bowed before Joab and ran. Again Achimaas son of Zadok said to Joab, “What prevents me from running after Cushi as well?” Joab said, “Why do you want to run, my son? Come here; you will not be the bearer of good news.” He replied, “But what if I run?” And he said to him, “Run.” So Achimaas ran by the shortcut and passed Cushi.

David was sitting between the two gates, while the watchman on the roof of the gate above the wall raised his eyes and saw a man running alone. He cried out and reported it to the king. The king said, “If he is alone, good news is in his mouth.” As the man hurried and drew nearer, the watchman saw another man running and cried out from the height, “I see another man running alone.” The king said, “This one too is a bearer of good news.” [Col. 0545A] The watchman said, “I observe the course of the first, which resembles the course of Achimaas son of Zadok.” The king said, “He is a good man, and he comes bearing good news.”

Achimaas cried out and said to the king, “Hail, O king.” He bowed before the king, falling prostrate on the ground, and said, “Blessed is the Lord your God, who has shut up the men who raised their hands against my lord the king.” The king said, “Is there peace for the boy Absalom?” Achimaas replied, “I saw a great tumult when your servant Joab sent me, your servant, O king; I know nothing else.” The king said to him, “Pass on and stand here.” When he had passed on and stood there, Cushi appeared. Coming, he said, “I bring good news, my lord the king; for today the Lord has judged in your favor against all who rose up against you.” [Col. 0545B] The king said to Cushi, “Is there peace for the boy Absalom?” Cushi answered, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against him for evil, become as that boy.”

The king was deeply grieved, went up to the upper room of the gate, and wept. And as he went he spoke thus: “My son Absalom, Absalom my son! Who will grant that I might die for you, Absalom my son, my son Absalom?”

(Chapter XIX.) It was reported to Joab that the king was weeping and mourning for his son. And the victory was turned into mourning for all the people on that day, for the people heard it said, “The king grieves over his son.” The people therefore refrained from entering the city on that day, as people usually refrain when they have been turned and flee from battle. The king covered his head and cried out in a loud voice, “My son Absalom, Absalom my son.”

Joab entered the king’s house and said, “Today you have put to shame the faces of all your servants who saved your life, and the lives of your sons and daughters, and the lives of your wives and concubines. You love those who hate you and hate those who love you; and today you have shown that you care nothing for your commanders or your servants. Truly I know now that if Absalom were alive and all of us had fallen, it would please you. Now therefore arise, go out, and speak to your servants and satisfy them. For I swear to you by the Lord that if you do not go out, not one person will remain with you tonight; and this will be worse for you than all the evils that have come upon you from your youth until now.”

The king therefore arose and sat at the gate, and it was reported to all the people that the king was sitting at the gate. Then all the multitude came before the king. Israel, however, fled to its tents. R. Amen.

Antiphon 1. Those who guarded my life took counsel together, saying: “God has abandoned him; pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to deliver him.” My God, do not withdraw from me; my God, attend to my help. V. O God, in you I have hoped; O Lord, I shall not be put to shame forever.

Prayer. God of hosts, although you were God, you willingly allowed yourself to be seized at the time of your Passion, while they plotted against you, saying, “Let him save himself, if he wishes.” Do not abandon us in our tribulation, and do not withdraw us from you, so that you alone may look upon us for our help—you who, on your Cross, triumph over the powers of this world. [Col. 0546A] R. Amen.

Antiphon 2. For forty years I was near this generation, and I said, “They always err in their heart.” To them I swore in my anger, “They shall not enter into my rest.” V. There your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works.

Prayer. O Lord, who were near your people for forty years, grant to your Church, which you acquired at the price of your blood, that they may not err in heart; but fill her with the infusion of the Holy Spirit and join her to yourself in eternal blessedness. R. Amen.

[Col. 0546B] Antiphon 3. My enemies live and have grown stronger against me; they have multiplied against me. Do not abandon me. R. Attend to my soul and deliver it; rescue me because of my enemies.

Hymn. “O Nazarene, light.” fol. 144.

Prayer. Your enemies, O Lord, live in punishments—those whom you destroyed by the power of the Cross. Therefore let those who were once bound by the glory of your Passion no longer grow strong against your Church, so that your members, rescued by the banner of the Cross, may gain victory over the enemy and seek the desired profit from the spoils of their foes.

Our Father.

At Vespers.

Praise. “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”

[Col. 0546C] Antiphon. I cried to you, O Lord, and said: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. Bring me out of prison.” Psalm 141.

Praise. “How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.” V. Reward your servant; I shall live, and I shall keep your words.

Hymn. “The Word of the Father.” fol. 252.

Capitulum. “Gloriously powerful.” fol. 264.

Praise. “I have practiced judgment.” fol. 296.

## FRIDAY

At Matins.

Antiphon. Many say to my soul, “There is no salvation for him in his God.” But you, O Lord, are my protector. Psalm 3.

[Col. 0546D] Prayer. “They have multiplied, O Lord.” fol. 170.

Antiphon 1. May it please you, O Lord, to deliver me; O Lord, look to my help. Let all who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame; let those who devise evil against me turn back and blush. V. Let those who say to me, “Well done, well done,” immediately bear their confusion. The Gloria is not said.

Prayer. May it please you, O Lord, to deliver us from the hand of our enemies; let those who seek to swallow us be confounded and put to shame. Come to our help, you who became our helper, so that we may not be put to shame in deeds of wickedness, having believed that we were renewed by the glory of your Passion. R. Amen.

Antiphon 2. My enemies spoke evil against me and surrounded me with words of hatred. Because I loved them, they opposed me; but I prayed for them. [Col. 0547A] V. You are God, O Lord; show me mercy for your name’s sake, for your mercy is gracious.

Prayer. Your enemies, O Lord, spoke evil against you, especially when they praised you, the supreme good, with deceitful flattery. Therefore, since you allowed yourself to be surrounded and attacked by their hateful words, we now humbly ask you to receive the prayers of our confession. R. Amen.

Antiphon 3. They took counsel together, saying, “Pursue him and seize him, for there is no one to rescue him from our hands.” Do not withdraw from me; attend to my help. V. Let those who seek my soul in order to take it be confounded and put to shame together. [Col. 0547B]

Prayer. Jesus, Son of God, when the impious crowd of the wicked pursued you vainly and plotted to seize you, it drove away from itself the benefit of your mercy; while striving to seize you by destroying your life, they did not know that you were the author of life. Grant that we may pursue in good works, with devout dedication, you whom they persecuted with wicked intent, so that where there will be perpetual mourning for your enemies, there may be perpetual joy for us. 323 R. Amen.

R. The tongue of the wicked became deceitful in their mouth, and all spoke falsehood. They lay in wait for blood; they hunted a righteous man to death. P. But he spoke peaceful words to them. [Col. 0547C] V. All the rulers of Judah gathered against the righteous man and seized him, saying, “Let this man die.” P. He himself. The Gloria is not said.

Prayer. Christ, ineffable Word of God the Father, before whom the tongue of the wicked is deceitful, when they committed a monstrous crime by shedding innocent blood: grant your Church a peaceful word, so that we who strive to overcome the world by your example may deserve to see heaven after our passage from this life. R. Amen.

At Lauds.

Antiphon. A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, do not despise. Have mercy on me, O God. Psalm 50.

Prayer. O God, who see all things and loosen our tongue: [as] the penitent meditates upon the fiftieth psalm, full of remedies, Just as you washed away David’s sins after the shedding of the blood of Uriah the Hittite through a contrite and humbled heart, so may you deign to cleanse our offenses through our satisfaction. R. Amen.

Antiphon. You know, O Lord; remember me; protect me from those who persecute me. Know that I have endured reproach for you.

Canticle of Jeremiah (Chapter XV).

You know, O Lord; remember me and visit me, * and protect me from those who persecute me.

Do not take me away in your patience; * know that I have endured reproach for you.

Your words were found, and I consumed them, and your word became for me the joy and gladness of my heart, * because your name was invoked over me, O Lord, God of hosts.

I did not sit in the assembly of those at play, and I gloried before your hand; * I sat alone, because you filled me with threat.

Why has my pain become perpetual, and my wound incurable, refusing to be healed? * It has become for me like deceitful waters without faithfulness.

Therefore thus says the Lord: * If you turn back, I will turn you back, and you shall stand before our face.

And if you separate the precious from the worthless, * you shall be like my mouth.

They shall turn to you, * and you shall not turn to them.

And I will make you for this people a strong bronze wall; [Col. 0548B] * they shall fight against you, but they shall not prevail, because I am with you to save you and deliver you, says the Lord.

And I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked, * and redeem you from the hand of the strong.

Prayer. Remember us, O Lord, and protect us from those who persecute us—you who endured the reproach of the Cross for us—so that in the very thing in which you willingly became bitter for us, we may here and forever rejoice in happiness. R. Amen.

Matutinarium. “In the morning you shall hear my voice, O Lord. In the morning I shall stand before you and see.” V. “Give ear to my words, O Lord; understand my cry.”

Praise. “Let the heavens of heavens and the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.” Psalm 148.

[Col. 0548C] Reading from the Book of Samuel (II Kings, Chapter XIX).

In those days: King David sent to Zadok and Abiathar the priests, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah, saying: Why are you the last to come to bring the king back to his house?” (The whole speech of Israel had reached the king in his house.) For the king had said, “You shall say this to the people: ‘You are my brothers, my bone and my flesh. Why are you the last to bring back the king?’ And say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my bone and my flesh? May God do this to me and add this also, if you are not commander of the army before me all the days in place of Joab.’”

And he inclined the heart of all the men of Judah as the heart of one man, and they sent to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.” So the king returned and came as far as the Jordan. All Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and bring him across the Jordan. Shimei son of Gera, son of Jemini, from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David, with a thousand men from Benjamin, and Ziba, the servant of Saul’s household, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They crossed the Jordan before the king and went through the fords to bring the king’s household across and to do according to his command.

When Shimei son of Gera had crossed the Jordan, he fell before the king and said to him, “Do not charge me, my lord, with iniquity, and do not remember the wrong done by your servant on the day when you, my lord the king, went out from Jerusalem; do not set it in your heart, O king. For your servant acknowledges his sin, and therefore today I have come first of all the house of Joseph to meet my lord the king.”

Abishai son of Zeruiah answered and said, “Shall Shimei not be put to death for these words, because he cursed the Lord’s anointed?” David said, “What is this to me and to you, son of Zeruiah, that you become Satan against me today? Shall a man be killed in Israel today? Or do I not know that today I have become king over Israel?” The king said to Shimei, “You shall not die,” and he swore this to him.

Mephibosheth, son of Saul, also came down to meet the king, with unwashed feet and an untrimmed beard. He had not washed his clothes from the day the king went out until the day of his peaceful return. When he came to meet the king, the king said to him, “Why did you not go with me, Mephibosheth?” He answered, “My lord the king, my servant despised me. I, your servant, told him to saddle an ass for me, so that I might mount it and go with the king, for I, your servant, am lame. Moreover, he accused me, your servant, to you, my lord the king. But you, my lord the king, are like an angel of God; do what seems good to you.

For all my father’s house was liable to death before my lord the king, but you placed your servant among the guests at your table. What further right have I to complain, or what can I cry out further to the king?” The king said to him, “Why do you speak further? What I have said is fixed: you and Ziba shall divide the possessions.” Mephibosheth answered the king, “Let him take everything, since my lord the king has returned peacefully to his house.”

Barzillai the Gileadite, a very old man, came down from Rogelim and brought the king across the Jordan, prepared also to accompany him beyond the river. Barzillai the Gileadite was very old, that is, eighty years old, and he himself had supplied food to the king while he stayed in the camp, for he was an exceedingly wealthy man. The king said to Barzillai, “Come with me, so that you may rest securely in Jerusalem.” Barzillai said to the king, “How many days of the years of my life remain, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem? I am eighty years old today. Are my senses still vigorous enough to distinguish sweet from bitter? Can food or drink delight your servant? Or can I still hear the voice of singers and singing women? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?

Your servant will go a little way with you from the Jordan. I do not need this exchange; but I ask that your servant may return, die in my city, and be buried beside the tomb of my father and my mother. Here is your servant Chamaam; let him go with you, my lord the king, and do for him whatever seems good to you.” The king said to him, “Let Chamaam cross with me, and I will do for him whatever pleases you; and whatever you ask of me, you shall obtain.”

When all the people and the king had crossed the Jordan, the king stopped, kissed Barzillai, and blessed him; and he returned to his own place. The king then crossed to Gilgal, and Chamaam with him. All the people of Judah had brought the king across, but only half of the people of Israel were present.
